statement.t: I am a member of one body of reasoning beings, made for a shared life with them.

statement.kind: Many pictures, one claim; then its consequences
statement.form: The statement gathers claims 1 and 2. Claim 1 is fused from four passages that use different pictures: body, city, sunlight, soul; claim 2 from four that say what we are made for. Claims 3 and 4 are what Marcus draws from it; the “because” of claim 5 is the editor’s.

seneca.becomes: With Seneca, the two central claims gain a second author, the body picture gains an arch beside it, and the article gains a concrete act, a second exercise and a caution about crowds: I may step back from them, but I must not hate them. He disputes none of Marcus’s claims here.
seneca.statement: The statement stands. With Seneca it gains the arch: we do not only belong together, we hold one another up.

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: we are the parts of one great body
piece.follows: We are all parts of one great body.
piece.context: Seneca’s short rule for how to treat other people, given after the rule for worshipping the gods. “We” is gods and humans together: all that you see is one.
gives: as limbs share one body

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: Nature produced us related to one another, since she created us from the same source and to the same end. She engendered in us mutual affection, and made us prone to friendships.
piece.follows: Nature made us kin, from one source and for one end, and gave us affection for one another.
piece.context: Seneca’s short rule for how to treat other people, given after the rule for worshipping the gods. “Us” is all human beings; “she” is Nature.
gives: We are made
for one another

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: no one can live happily who has regard to himself alone and transforms everything into a question of his own utility; you must live for your neighbour, if you would live for yourself
piece.follows: No one lives happily for himself alone; to live for myself I have to live for another.
piece.context: Opens on friendship (a friend’s interest is mine), then widens to all fellow men in 48.3. “Your neighbour” is any other person, the friend first.
gives: that shared life is our own good

items.label: why
items.t: We hold one another up as the stones of an arch do: without that support the arch falls.
items.why: Marcus has body, city, sunlight and soul. The arch adds something none of them states: that the whole stands only because its parts hold one another up.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: Our relations with one another are like a stone arch, which would collapse if the stones did not mutually support each other
support.follows: Human fellowship stands the way a stone arch does: only because its parts support one another.
support.context: Seneca’s short rule for how to treat other people, given after the rule for worshipping the gods. “Our relations with one another” is human fellowship as a whole, not one friendship.

items.label: action
items.t: My hands should be ready for anyone who needs help.
items.why: Marcus’s claim says to aim at the common good. Seneca names what that looks like when someone is in front of me.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: Through her orders, let our hands be ready for all that needs to be helped
support.follows: By Nature’s order we should be ready to help whatever needs help.
support.context: The practical close of Seneca’s short rule for how to treat other people. “Her” is Nature; those to be helped are people in need, like the shipwrecked and the starving just named.

items.label: practice
items.t: I shall keep one line in my heart and on my lips: I am human, and nothing human is foreign to me.
items.why: A second exercise beside Marcus’s own. The line is from the playwright Terence; Seneca quotes it as something to repeat.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: Let this verse be in your heart and on your lips: I am a man; and nothing in man’s lot Do I deem foreign to me.
support.follows: I should keep ready a line that says nothing human is foreign to me.
support.context: Seneca’s short rule for how to treat other people, given after the rule for worshipping the gods. “This verse” is a line of Terence, unnamed here, that Lucilius is told to keep ready.

items.label: breaks
items.t: I should not hate the many for being unlike me. I may withdraw into myself as far as I can, and keep the company that makes me better and that I can make better.
items.why: Marcus says that hating cuts me off. Seneca, writing about crowds that unsettle a character not yet firm, forbids the hatred and still advises stepping back. He does not speak of cutting off, so this is an addition, not a dispute.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: nor should you hate the many because they are unlike you. Withdraw into yourself, as far as you can. Associate with those who will make a better man of you. Welcome those whom you yourself can improve.
support.follows: I should not hate the crowd for being unlike me; I should withdraw into myself as far as I can and keep company that improves me and that I can improve.
support.context: A letter on avoiding crowds, which unsettle a character not yet firm. “The many” is the crowd, as at the games; “withdraw” is from it, not from everyone.

passages.title: On the usefulness of basic principles
passages.text: all that you behold, that which comprises both god and man, is one—we are the parts of one great body. Nature produced us related to one another, since she created us from the same source and to the same end. She engendered in us mutual affection, and made us prone to friendships. She established fairness and justice; according to her ruling, it is more wretched to commit than to suffer injury. Through her orders, let our hands be ready for all that needs to be helped.

passages.title: On quibbling as unworthy of the philosopher
passages.text: But the fact is, the same thing is advantageous to me which is advantageous to you; for I am not your friend unless whatever is at issue concerning you is my concern also. Friendship produces between us a partnership in all our interests. There is no such thing as good or bad fortune for the individual; we live in common. And no one can live happily who has regard to himself alone and transforms everything into a question of his own utility; you must live for your neighbour, if you would live for yourself.

passages.title: On the usefulness of basic principles
passages.text: Let this verse be in your heart and on your lips: I am a man; and nothing in man’s lot Do I deem foreign to me. Let us possess things in common; for birth is ours in common. Our relations with one another are like a stone arch, which would collapse if the stones did not mutually support each other, and which is upheld in this very way.

passages.title: On crowds
passages.text: But both courses are to be avoided; you should not copy the bad simply because they are many, nor should you hate the many because they are unlike you. Withdraw into yourself, as far as you can. Associate with those who will make a better man of you. Welcome those whom you yourself can improve. The process is mutual; for men learn while they teach.

claims.t: Everything that reasons shares one reason, as limbs share one body, citizens one city, and every lit place one sun.
claims.shared: Four pictures (body, city, sunlight, soul) with one structure: a single thing present in many, and not split by being shared.
claims.changed: Marcus says soul, reason and intellectual soul by turns. The fused claim says “reason” throughout.

support.quote:
As several members in one body united, so are reasonable creatures
in a body divided and dispersed
support.follows: Reasoning beings relate to one another as the parts of one body do.
gives: as limbs share one body

then are we fellow-citizens. If so, then are we partners in some one
commonweal. If so, then the world is as it were a city.
support.follows: We are fellow citizens, partners in one commonwealth, and the world is like a city.
gives: citizens one city
support.note: The last step of a chain that starts from reason being common to all.

support.quote:

support.quote:
of all that are reasonable, but one reasonable soul, divided betwixt

claims.t: We are made for one another and for one common work, and that shared life is our own good.
claims.shared: Each says that a reasonable being is directed toward its own kind, whether by its making (7.10, 9.21, 5.15) or by its nature (9.7). 5.15 and 9.7 both say the direction is toward one another, and 5.15 and 7.10 both call it its own good.

support.quote:
all made and prepared for one common
operation
support.follows: All are made and prepared for one shared work.
gives: for one common work
We are made

support.quote:
As thou thyself, whoever thou art, were made for the perfection and
consummation, being a member of it, of a common society
support.follows: I was made to complete a shared society, as one of its members.
gives: We are made

support.quote:
Whatsoever therefore is partaker of that reasonable common
nature, naturally doth as much and more long after his own kind.
support.follows: Whatever shares in reason is naturally drawn to others who share in it.
gives: for one another

support.quote: Society therefore is the proper good of a rational creature.
support.follows: Living with others is what is good for a reasoning being.
gives: that shared life is our own good

support.quote:
For that we
are made for society, it hath long since been demonstrated.
support.follows: It has already been shown that we are made for society.
gives: We are made

support.quote:
those things that are best, are made one for another? And those things
that have souls, are better than those that have none? and of those that
have, those best that have rational souls?
support.follows: The best things are made for one another, and the best of all are those with reasoning souls.
gives: We are made
for one another
support.note: Asked as questions no one can answer with no: the best things are made for one another, and the best are those with reasoning souls.

support.quote: as doing good to thyself, when thou dost good unto others
support.follows: When I do good to others, I do good to myself.
gives: our own good
support.note: The good of the other and my own are the same act.

claims.t: So each thing I do should aim at the common good, directly or at a distance, and holding to that one aim is what makes me one person.
claims.shared: Two passages draw the same consequence from membership: the aim of action is common. 11.19 adds what the single aim does for the one who holds it.

support.quote:
so must every
action of thine tend to the perfection and consummation of a life that
is truly sociable
support.follows: Every action of mine should help make shared life complete.
gives: each thing I do should aim at the common good

support.quote:
What action soever of thine therefore that either
immediately or afar off, hath not reference to the common good, that is
an exorbitant and disorderly action
support.follows: An action with no connection to the common good is out of order, even when the connection would only be distant.
gives: directly or at a distance
aim at the common good

support.quote:
so must the end also that we propose unto ourselves, be common
and sociable
support.follows: The goal I set for myself should be a common one.
gives: aim at the common good

support.quote:
he that doth direct all his own private motions and
purposes to that end, all his actions will be agreeable and uniform; and
by that means will be still the same man
support.follows: A person who directs all his purposes to that one end acts consistently and stays the same person.
gives: holding to that one aim is what makes me one person

claims.t: When I hate someone, wrong them, or resent what happens, I cut myself off, and not from that one thing only but from the whole.
claims.shared: Three pictures of severing (a branch, a limb, a faction). In each the person does it to himself, and in each the cut is from the whole.

support.quote:
he that hates and is averse, cuts himself off from his
neighbour
support.follows: Hatred and aversion are how a person cuts himself off from a neighbour.
gives: When I hate someone

support.quote:
and knows not that at the same time he divides himself from

support.follows: In the same act, and without knowing it, he separates himself from the whole body of people.
gives: from the whole

support.quote:
If ever thou sawest either a hand, or a foot, or a head lying by

such must thou conceive him to make himself, as much as in him lieth,
that either is offended with anything that is happened
support.follows: A person who resents anything that has happened makes himself, as far as he can, like a hand or foot cut off from the body.
gives: resent what happens

support.quote:
or that commits anything
against the natural law of mutual correspondence, and society among men
support.follows: Acting against the natural law of fellowship among people is counted as the same kind of act.
gives: wrong them

support.quote:
he needed not, except he would himself, have divided
himself from the whole
support.follows: A person is divided from the whole only by his own will.
gives: I cut myself off
from the whole

support.quote:
as one among
the people who from such and such a consent and unity, should factiously

support.follows: It is like a man who breaks away from a united people to form a faction.

claims.t: Having cut myself off, I can grow back into the whole, because nature is stronger than my leaving.
claims.shared: Two passages say the return is possible in almost the same words. 9.7 says something else: those who flee their nature are caught by it. Joining the two with “because” is the editor’s step.
claims.changed: Both 11.7 and 8.32 credit the return to God. The fused claim credits nature, following 9.7.

inferences.why: No passage gives this reason: 11.7 and 8.32 credit the return to God, and 9.7 speaks of flight from nature, not of return.

support.quote:
once cut off we may grow together
and become part of the whole again
support.follows: Once cut off, we can grow together again and be part of the whole again.
gives: I can grow back into the whole

support.quote:
if he would himself, he might return, and grow
together again
support.follows: Return is possible if the person wants it.
gives: I can grow back

support.quote:
But though they fly from nature, yet are they stopt in
their course, and apprehended.
support.follows: Reasoning beings cannot finally escape their nature; it catches up with them.
gives: nature is stronger than my leaving

single.quote:
use
thyself often to say to thyself, I am μέλος, or a member of the mass and
body of reasonable substances
single.label: A practice
single.t: I shall often say to myself: I am a member, and not merely a part.
single.why: Only 7.10 gives an exercise. It is kept as the article’s practice.
single.follows: I should often tell myself that I am a member of this body.

single.quote:
But if this happen often the misery
is that the further a man is run in this division, the harder he is to
be reunited and restored again
single.label: A warning
single.t: The more often I cut myself off, the harder the return.
single.why: Only 11.7 says the return gets harder. One witness, so it is not fused into claim 5.
single.follows: Each repeated separation makes reunion harder.

members.text:
Of all unreasonable creatures, there is but one unreasonable soul;
and of all that are reasonable, but one reasonable soul, divided betwixt
them all. As of all earthly things there is but one earth, and but one
light that we see by; and but one air that we breathe in, as many as
either breathe or see. Now whatsoever partakes of some common thing,
naturally affects and inclines unto that whereof it is part, being of
one kind and nature with it. Whatsoever is earthly, presseth downwards
to the common earth. Whatsoever is liquid, would flow together. And
whatsoever is airy, would be together likewise. So that without some
obstacle, and some kind of violence, they cannot well be kept asunder.
Whatsoever is fiery, doth not only by reason of the elementary fire tend
upwards; but here also is so ready to join, and to burn together, that
whatsoever doth want sufficient moisture to make resistance, is easily
set on fire. Whatsoever therefore is partaker of that reasonable common
nature, naturally doth as much and more long after his own kind. For by
how much in its own nature it excels all other things, by so much more
is it desirous to be joined and united unto that, which is of its own
nature. As for unreasonable creatures then, they had not long been, but
presently begun among them swarms, and flocks, and broods of young ones,
and a kind of mutual love and affection. For though but unreasonable,
yet a kind of soul these had, and therefore was that natural desire of
union more strong and intense in them, as in creatures of a more
excellent nature, than either in plants, or stones, or trees. But among
reasonable creatures, begun commonwealths, friendships, families, public
meetings, and even in their wars, conventions, and truces. Now among
them that were yet of a more excellent nature, as the stars and planets,
though by their nature far distant one from another, yet even among them
began some mutual correspondency and unity. So proper is it to
excellency in a high degree to affect unity, as that even in things so
far distant, it could operate unto a mutual sympathy. But now behold,
what is now come to pass. Those creatures that are reasonable, are now
the only creatures that have forgotten their natural affection and
inclination of one towards another. Among them alone of all other things
that are of one kind, there is not to be found a general disposition to
flow together. But though they fly from nature, yet are they stopt in
their course, and apprehended. Do they what they can, nature doth
prevail. And so shalt thou confess, if thou dost observe it. For sooner
mayst thou find a thing earthly, where no earthly thing is, than find a
man that naturally can live by himself alone.

Such as thy thoughts and ordinary cogitations are, such will thy
mind be in time. For the soul doth as it were receive its tincture from
the fancies, and imaginations. Dye it therefore and thoroughly soak it
with the assiduity of these cogitations. As for example. Wheresoever
thou mayest live, there it is in thy power to live well and happy. But
thou mayest live at the Court, there then also mayest thou live well and
happy. Again, that which everything is made for, he is also made unto
that, and cannot but naturally incline unto it. That which anything
doth naturally incline unto, therein is his end. Wherein the end of
everything doth consist, therein also doth his good and benefit consist.
Society therefore is the proper good of a rational creature. For that we
are made for society, it hath long since been demonstrated. Or can any
man make any question of this, that whatsoever is naturally worse and
inferior, is ordinarily subordinated to that which is better? and that
those things that are best, are made one for another? And those things
that have souls, are better than those that have none? and of those that
have, those best that have rational souls?

If ever thou sawest either a hand, or a foot, or a head lying by
itself, in some place or other, as cut off from the rest of the body,
such must thou conceive him to make himself, as much as in him lieth,
that either is offended with anything that is happened, (whatsoever it
be) and as it were divides himself from it: or that commits anything
against the natural law of mutual correspondence, and society among men:
or, he that, commits any act of uncharitableness. Whosoever thou art,
thou art such, thou art cast forth I know not whither out of the general
unity, which is according to nature. Thou went born indeed a part, but
now thou hast cut thyself off. However, herein is matter of joy and
exultation, that thou mayst be united again. God hath not granted
it unto any other part, that once separated and cut off, it might be
reunited, and come together again. But, behold, that GOODNESS how great
and immense it is! which hath so much esteemed MAN. As at first he
was so made, that he needed not, except he would himself, have divided
himself from the whole; so once divided and cut off, IT hath so provided
and ordered it, that if he would himself, he might return, and grow
together again, and be admitted into its former rank and place of a
part, as he was before.

As several members in one body united, so are reasonable creatures
in a body divided and dispersed, all made and prepared for one common
operation. And this thou shalt apprehend the better, if thou shalt use
thyself often to say to thyself, I am μέλος, or a member of the mass and
body of reasonable substances. But if thou shalt say I am μέρος, or
a part, thou dost not yet love men from thy heart. The joy that thou
takest in the exercise of bounty, is not yet grounded upon a due
ratiocination and right apprehension of the nature of things. Thou dost
exercise it as yet upon this ground barely, as a thing convenient and
fitting; not, as doing good to thyself, when thou dost good unto others.

If to understand and to be reasonable be common unto all men, then
is that reason, for which we are termed reasonable, common unto all. If
reason is general, then is that reason also, which prescribeth what is
to be done and what not, common unto all. If that, then law. If law,
then are we fellow-citizens. If so, then are we partners in some one
commonweal. If so, then the world is as it were a city. For which other
commonweal is it, that all men can be said to be members of? From this
common city it is, that understanding, reason, and law is derived unto
us, for from whence else? For as that which in me is earthly I have from
some common earth; and that which is moist from some other element is
imparted; as my breath and life hath its proper fountain; and that
likewise which is dry and fiery in me: (for there is nothing which doth
not proceed from something; as also there is nothing that can be reduced
unto mere nothing:) so also is there some common beginning from whence
my understanding hath proceeded.

As thou thyself, whoever thou art, were made for the perfection and
consummation, being a member of it, of a common society; so must every
action of thine tend to the perfection and consummation of a life that
is truly sociable. What action soever of thine therefore that either
immediately or afar off, hath not reference to the common good, that is
an exorbitant and disorderly action; yea it is seditious; as one among
the people who from such and such a consent and unity, should factiously
divide and separate himself.

There is but one light of the sun, though it be intercepted by
walls and mountains, and other thousand objects. There is but one common
substance of the whole world, though it be concluded and restrained into
several different bodies, in number infinite. There is but one common
soul, though divided into innumerable particular essences and natures.
So is there but one common intellectual soul, though it seem to be
divided. And as for all other parts of those generals which we have
mentioned, as either sensitive souls or subjects, these of themselves
(as naturally irrational) have no common mutual reference one unto
another, though many of them contain a mind, or reasonable faculty in
them, whereby they are ruled and governed. But of every reasonable mind,
this the particular nature, that it hath reference to whatsoever is
of her own kind, and desireth to be united: neither can this common
affection, or mutual unity and correspondency, be here intercepted or
divided, or confined to particulars as those other common things are.

He that hath not one and the self-same general end always as long
as he liveth, cannot possibly be one and the self-same man always. But
this will not suffice except thou add also what ought to be this general
end. For as the general conceit and apprehension of all those things
which upon no certain ground are by the greater part of men deemed good,
cannot be uniform and agreeable, but that only which is limited and
restrained by some certain proprieties and conditions, as of community:
that nothing be conceived good, which is not commonly and publicly
good: so must the end also that we propose unto ourselves, be common
and sociable. For he that doth direct all his own private motions and
purposes to that end, all his actions will be agreeable and uniform; and
by that means will be still the same man.

members.why: A wish to share one mind as we share one air. Close to claim 1, but a wish and not a statement.
members.text:
Not only now henceforth to have a common breath, or to hold
correspondency of breath, with that air, that compasseth us about; but
to have a common mind, or to hold correspondency of mind also with that
rational substance, which compasseth all things. For, that also is of
itself, and of its own nature (if a man can but draw it in as he should)
everywhere diffused; and passeth through all things, no less than the
air doth, if a man can but suck it in.

A branch cut off from the continuity of that which was next unto
it, must needs be cut off from the whole tree: so a man that is divided
from another man, is divided from the whole society. A branch is cut off
by another, but he that hates and is averse, cuts himself off from his
neighbour, and knows not that at the same time he divides himself from
the whole body, or corporation. But herein is the gift and mercy of God,
the Author of this society, in that, once cut off we may grow together
and become part of the whole again. But if this happen often the misery
is that the further a man is run in this division, the harder he is to
be reunited and restored again: and however the branch which, once cut
of afterwards was graffed in, gardeners can tell you is not like that
which sprouted together at first, and still continued in the unity of
the body.

decisions: Reads body, city, sunlight and soul as four pictures of one claim. Marcus sets sunlight beside soul himself (12.23, 9.7); body and city he never lines up with them.
Joins the return (11.7, 8.32) to 9.7 with “because”. Marcus states the return and credits it to God; he does not derive it.
Says “nature” where two of the three passages behind claim 5 say God.
articles.limit: Nine of the ten passages feed the article. That is also a risk: fusing smooths over differences. 4.4 argues for the unity step by step, and 9.7 argues from the elements; the article states the unity and keeps neither argument. Nine of the 22 components of its claims rest on two or more passages; the other thirteen are one passage’s words.

articles.title: The work that belongs to me

statement.t: My work is to let reason lead in how I treat other people, in how I handle my body, and in how I judge.
statement.form: Three passages (7.30, 8.25 and 8.6) each list what is proper to a human being, in different words and at different lengths. The statement and the three claims under “In action” come from aligning those lists item by item.

seneca.becomes: With Seneca, four of the five claims gain a second author and Practice gains a way to stay my own master amid business. To the claim about the body he adds that it may still be indulged somewhat.
seneca.statement: The statement stands. Seneca names its ground outright: reason is what is peculiar to a human being.

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: I am naturally born to love all men
piece.follows: I am born to love all human beings.
piece.context: Seneca argues that praise from good men is a good for the man praised; “I” is that good man, glad of it because he loves all people by nature.
gives: mean well by my own kind

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: I do not maintain that the body is not to be indulged at all; but I maintain that we must not be slaves to it
piece.follows: The body may be indulged somewhat, but we must not be its slaves.
piece.context: On our love of the body, which we must guard; “it” is the body, and the slavery he describes is living for it and fearing on its behalf.
gives: I do not let its urges rule me

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: our alliance shall nevertheless not be one of equality; the soul shall bring all quarrels before its own tribunal
piece.follows: While soul and body are joined they are not equals: the soul judges every dispute between them.
piece.context: Seneca refuses to live as his body’s chattel; “our alliance” is the soul’s with the body while they are bound together. A resolve, not a law of nature.
gives: Reason was made to be in charge of the body

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: And what is it which this reason demands of him? The easiest thing in the world,—to live in accordance with his own nature
piece.follows: What reason asks of a human being is to live by his own nature.
piece.context: Seneca has just said a man’s own good is reason perfected in the soul; “his own nature” is the nature of man as a reasoning animal.
gives: living according to my own nature

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: What then is peculiar to man? Reason. When this is right and has reached perfection, man’s felicity is complete.
piece.follows: Reason is what is peculiar to a human being; when it is right and perfected, his happiness is complete.
piece.context: Each thing is judged by the good that is its own, as a stag by speed; “this” is reason, and he speaks of reason made perfect, not of work under way.
gives: doing it makes me content

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: the wise man regards the reason for all his actions, but not the results. The beginning is in our own power; fortune decides the issue
piece.follows: The wise man looks to the reasons for what he does, not to how it turns out: the start is ours, the outcome is fortune’s.
piece.context: Seneca has admitted that a careful life cannot guarantee safety; “the results” are how the wise man’s actions turn out, which fortune decides.
gives: not its result

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: Because of his poverty he is prevented from showing how the State should be handled; but he teaches, none the less, how poverty should be handled.
piece.follows: Kept by poverty from showing how a state should be handled, the wise man shows how poverty should be handled.
piece.context: Seneca answers that hardship cannot stop the wise man as a storm stops a pilot; “he” is the wise man, whom poverty keeps out of public life.
gives: when something blocks one action, dealing with that obstacle becomes my next action

items.label: practice
items.t: I lend myself to my affairs; I do not hand myself over to them.
items.why: Marcus says to keep to the three things and not be distracted. Seneca, writing about keeping time for study, says how he stays his own master amid business.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: I do not surrender myself to my affairs, but loan myself to them
support.follows: I can take part in business without giving myself up to it.
support.context: Seneca denies that business keeps anyone from study; “my affairs” are his engagements, and what he keeps back is his time and his own thoughts.

amend.t: ; I may still indulge it somewhat

passages.title: On the intimations of our immortality
passages.text: The retort comes: “But whose good is this renown, this praise rendered to a good man by good men? Is it of the one praised, or of the one who praises?” Of both, I say. It is my own good, in that I am praised, because I am naturally born to love all men, and I rejoice in having done good deeds and congratulate myself on having found men who express their ideas of my virtues with gratitude; that they are grateful, is a good to the many, but it is a good to me also. For my spirit is so ordered that I can regard the good of other men as my own—in any case those of whose good I am myself the cause.

passages.title: On the reasons for withdrawing from the world
passages.text: I confess that we all have an inborn affection for our body; I confess that we are entrusted with its guardianship. I do not maintain that the body is not to be indulged at all; but I maintain that we must not be slaves to it. He will have many masters who makes his body his master, who is over-fearful in its behalf, who judges everything according to the body.

passages.title: On the first cause
passages.text: Never shall this flesh drive me to feel fear, or to assume any pretence that is unworthy of a good man. Never shall I lie in order to honour this petty body. When it seems proper, I shall sever my connexion with it. And at present, while we are bound together, our alliance shall nevertheless not be one of equality; the soul shall bring all quarrels before its own tribunal. To despise our bodies is sure freedom.

passages.title: On the god within us
passages.text: And what is it which this reason demands of him? The easiest thing in the world,—to live in accordance with his own nature. But this is turned into a hard task by the general madness of mankind; we push one another into vice. And how can a man be recalled to salvation, when he has none to restrain him, and all mankind to urge him on? Farewell.

passages.title: On learning wisdom in old age
passages.text: What then is peculiar to man? Reason. When this is right and has reached perfection, man’s felicity is complete. Hence, if everything is praiseworthy and has arrived at the end intended by its nature, when it has brought its peculiar good to perfection, and if man’s peculiar good is reason; then, if a man has brought his reason to perfection, he is praiseworthy and has reached the end suited to his nature. This perfect reason is called virtue, and is likewise that which is honourable.

passages.title: On the reasons for withdrawing from the world
passages.text: And finally, the wise man regards the reason for all his actions, but not the results. The beginning is in our own power; fortune decides the issue, but I do not allow her to pass sentence upon myself. You may say: “But she can inflict a measure of suffering and of trouble.” The highwayman does not pass sentence when he slays.

passages.title: On some vain syllogisms
passages.text: Besides, he is not prevented from helping others, even at the time when constraining circumstances press him down. Because of his poverty he is prevented from showing how the State should be handled; but he teaches, none the less, how poverty should be handled. His work goes on throughout his whole life. Thus no fortune, no external circumstance, can shut off the wise man from action. For the very thing which engages his attention prevents him from attending to other things. He is ready for either outcome: if it brings goods, he controls them; if evils, he conquers them.

passages.title: On good company
passages.text: We are deceived by those who would have us believe that a multitude of affairs blocks their pursuit of liberal studies; they make a pretence of their engagements, and multiply them, when their engagements are merely with themselves. As for me, Lucilius, my time is free; it is indeed free, and wherever I am, I am master of myself. For I do not surrender myself to my affairs, but loan myself to them, and I do not hunt out excuses for wasting my time. And wherever I am situated, I carry on my own meditations and ponder in my mind some wholesome thought.

members.text:
Reason, and rational power, are faculties which content themselves
with themselves, and their own proper operations. And as for their first
inclination and motion, that they take from themselves. But their
progress is right to the end and object, which is in their way, as it
were, and lieth just before them: that is, which is feasible and
possible, whether it be that which at the first they proposed to
themselves, or no. For which reason also such actions are termed
κατορθώσεις, to intimate the directness of the way, by which they are
achieved. Nothing must be thought to belong to a man, which doth not
belong unto him as he is a man. These, the event of purposes, are not
things required in a man. The nature of man doth not profess any such
things. The final ends and consummations of actions are nothing at all
to a man's nature. The end therefore of a man, or the _summum bonum_
whereby that end is fulfilled, cannot consist in the consummation of
actions purposed and intended. Again, concerning these outward worldly
things, were it so that any of them did properly belong unto man, then
would it not belong unto man, to condemn them and to stand in opposition
with them. Neither would he be praiseworthy that can live without them;
or he good, (if these were good indeed) who of his own accord doth
deprive himself of any of them. But we see contrariwise, that the more a
man doth withdraw himself from these wherein external pomp and greatness
doth consist, or any other like these; or the better he doth bear with
the loss of these, the better he is accounted.

Every particular nature hath content, when in its own proper course
it speeds. A reasonable nature doth then speed, when first in matter of
fancies and imaginations, it gives no consent to that which is either
false uncertain. Secondly, when in all its motions and resolutions it
takes its level at the common good only, and that it desireth nothing,
and flieth from nothing, bet what is in its own power to compass or
avoid. And lastly, when it willingly and gladly embraceth, whatsoever is
dealt and appointed unto it by the common nature. For it is part of it;
even as the nature of any one leaf, is part of the common nature of all
plants and trees. But that the nature of a leaf, is part of a nature
both unreasonable and unsensible, and which in its proper end may be
hindered; or, which is servile and slavish: whereas the nature of man is
part of a common nature which cannot be hindered, and which is both
reasonable and just. From whence also it is, that according to the
worth of everything, she doth make such equal distribution of all
things, as of duration, substance form, operation, and of events and
accidents. But herein consider not whether thou shalt find this equality
in everything absolutely and by itself; but whether in all the
particulars of some one thing taken together, and compared with all the
particulars of some other thing, and them together likewise.

Look not about upon other men's minds and understandings; but look
right on forwards whither nature, both that of the universe, in those
things that happen unto thee; and thine in particular, in those things
that are done by thee: doth lead, and direct thee. Now every one is
bound to do that, which is consequent and agreeable to that end which
by his true natural constitution he was ordained unto. As for all other
things, they are ordained for the use of reasonable creatures: as in all
things we see that that which is worse and inferior, is made for
that which is better. Reasonable creatures, they are ordained one for
another. That therefore which is chief in every man's constitution, is,
that he intend the common good. The second is, that he yield not to any
lusts and motions of the flesh. For it is the part and privilege of the
reasonable and intellective faculty, that she can so bound herself,
as that neither the sensitive, nor the appetitive faculties, may not
anyways prevail upon her. For both these are brutish. And therefore over
both she challengeth mastery, and cannot anyways endure, if in her right
temper, to be subject unto either. And this indeed most justly. For
by nature she was ordained to command all in the body. The third
thing proper to man by his constitution, is, to avoid all rashness and
precipitancy; and not to be subject to error. To these things then, let
the mind apply herself and go straight on, without any distraction about
other things, and she hath her end, and by consequent her happiness.

members.why: The elements keep their place; the mind that resents does not. An argument for submission, nearer to Article 3.
members.text:
What portion soever, either of air or fire there be in thee,
although by nature it tend upwards, submitting nevertheless to the
ordinance of the universe, it abides here below in this mixed body. So
whatsoever is in thee, either earthy, or humid, although by nature it
tend downwards, yet is it against its nature both raised upwards, and
standing, or consistent. So obedient are even the elements themselves to
the universe, abiding patiently wheresoever (though against their
nature) they are placed, until the sound as it were of their retreat,
and separation. Is it not a grievous thing then, that thy reasonable
part only should be disobedient, and should not endure to keep its
place: yea though it be nothing enjoined that is contrary unto it, but
that only which is according to its nature? For we cannot say of it when
it is disobedient, as we say of the fire, or air, that it tends upwards
towards its proper element, for then goes it the quite contrary way. For
the motion of the mind to any injustice, or incontinency, or to sorrow,
or to fear, is nothing else but a separation from nature. Also when the
mind is grieved for anything that is happened by the divine providence,
then doth it likewise forsake its own place. For it was ordained unto
holiness and godliness, which specially consist in an humble submission
to God and His providence in all things; as well as unto justice: these
also being part of those duties, which as naturally sociable, we are
bound unto; and without which we cannot happily converse one with
another: yea and the very ground and fountain indeed of all just
actions.

After one consideration, man is nearest unto us; as we are bound
to do them good, and to bear with them. But as he may oppose any of our
true proper actions, so man is unto me but as a thing indifferent: even
as the sun, or the wind, or some wild beast. By some of these it may be,
that some operation or other of mine, may be hindered; however, of my
mind and resolution itself, there can be no let or impediment, by reason
of that ordinary constant both exception (or reservation wherewith it
inclineth) and ready conversion of objects; from that which may not be,
to that which may be, which in the prosecution of its inclinations, as
occasion serves, it doth observe. For by these the mind doth turn and
convert any impediment whatsoever, to be her aim and purpose. So that
what before was the impediment, is now the principal object of her
working; and that which before was in her way, is now her readiest way.

The true joy of a man, is to do that which properly belongs unto a
man. That which is most proper unto a man, is, first, to be kindly
affected towards them that are of the same kind and nature as he is
himself to contemn all sensual motions and appetites, to discern rightly
all plausible fancies and imaginations, to contemplate the nature of the
universe; both it, and things that are done in it. In which kind of
contemplation three several relations are to be observed The first, to
the apparent secondary cause. The Second to the first original cause,
God, from whom originally proceeds whatsoever doth happen in the world.
The third and last, to them that we live and converse with: what use may
be made of it, to their use and benefit.

As almost all her other faculties and properties the nature of
the universe hath imparted unto every reasonable creature, so this in
particular we have received from her, that as whatsoever doth oppose
itself unto her, and doth withstand her in her purposes and intentions,
she doth, though against its will and intention, bring it about to
herself, to serve herself of it in the execution of her own destinated
ends; and so by this though not intended co-operation of it with herself
makes it part of herself whether it will or no. So may every reasonable
creature, what crosses and impediments soever it meets with in the
course of this mortal life, it may use them as fit and proper objects,
to the furtherance of whatsoever it intended and absolutely proposed
unto itself as its natural end and happiness.

As long as the foot doth that which belongeth unto it to do, and
the hand that which belongs unto it, their labour, whatsoever it be, is
not unnatural. So a man as long as he doth that which is proper unto
a man, his labour cannot be against nature; and if it be not against
nature, then neither is it hurtful unto him. But if it were so that
happiness did consist in pleasure: how came notorious robbers, impure
abominable livers, parricides, and tyrants, in so large a measure to
have their part of pleasures?

That inward mistress part of man if it be in its own true natural
temper, is towards all worldly chances and events ever so disposed and
affected, that it will easily turn and apply itself to that which may
be, and is within its own power to compass, when that cannot be which at
first it intended. For it never doth absolutely addict and apply itself
to any one object, but whatsoever it is that it doth now intend and
prosecute, it doth prosecute it with exception and reservation; so that
whatsoever it is that falls out contrary to its first intentions, even
that afterwards it makes its proper object. Even as the fire when it
prevails upon those things that are in his way; by which things indeed a
little fire would have been quenched, but a great fire doth soon turn to
its own nature, and so consume whatsoever comes in his way: yea by those
very things it is made greater and greater.

It is not possible that any nature should be inferior unto art,
since that all arts imitate nature. If this be so; that the most perfect
and general nature of all natures should in her operation come short of
the skill of arts, is most improbable. Now common is it to all arts, to
make that which is worse for the better's sake. Much more then doth the
common nature do the same. Hence is the first ground of justice. From
justice all other virtues have their existence. For justice cannot be
preserved, if either we settle our minds and affections upon worldly
things; or be apt to be deceived, or rash, and inconstant.

members.why: A long passage that calls injustice, lying and pleasure-seeking impious. It argues for the same three works from piety, a ground the article does not use.
members.text:
He that is unjust, is also impious. For the nature of the universe,
having made all reasonable creatures one for another, to the end that
they should do one another good; more or less according to the several
persons and occasions but in nowise hurt one another: it is manifest
that he that doth transgress against this her will, is guilty of impiety
towards the most ancient and venerable of all the deities. For the
nature of the universe, is the nature the common parent of all, and
therefore piously to be observed of all things that are, and that which
now is, to whatsoever first was, and gave it its being, hath relation
of blood and kindred. She is also called truth and is the first cause
of all truths. He therefore that willingly and wittingly doth lie, is
impious in that he doth receive, and so commit injustice: but he that
against his will, in that he disagreeth from the nature of the universe,
and in that striving with the nature of the world he doth in his
particular, violate the general order of the world. For he doth no
better than strive and war against it, who contrary to his own nature
applieth himself to that which is contrary to truth. For nature had
before furnished him with instincts and opportunities sufficient for the
attainment of it; which he having hitherto neglected, is not now able
to discern that which is false from that which is true. He also that
pursues after pleasures, as that which is truly good and flies from
pains, as that which is truly evil: is impious. For such a one must of
necessity oftentimes accuse that common nature, as distributing many
things both unto the evil, and unto the good, not according to the
deserts of either: as unto the bad oftentimes pleasures, and the causes
of pleasures; so unto the good, pains, and the occasions of pains.
Again, he that feareth pains and crosses in this world, feareth some of
those things which some time or other must needs happen in the world.
And that we have already showed to be impious. And he that pursueth
after pleasures, will not spare, to compass his desires, to do that
which is unjust, and that is manifestly impious. Now those things which
unto nature are equally indifferent (for she had not created both, both
pain and pleasure, if both had not been unto her equally indifferent):
they that will live according to nature, must in those things (as being
of the same mind and disposition that she is) be as equally indifferent.
Whosoever therefore in either matter of pleasure and pain; death and
life; honour and dishonour, (which things nature in the administration
of the world, indifferently doth make use of), is not as indifferent,
it is apparent that he is impious. When I say that common nature
doth indifferently make use of them, my meaning is, that they happen
indifferently in the ordinary course of things, which by a necessary
consequence, whether as principal or accessory, come to pass in the
world, according to that first and ancient deliberation of Providence,
by which she from some certain beginning, did resolve upon the creation
of such a world, conceiving then in her womb as it were some certain
rational generative seeds and faculties of things future, whether
subjects, changes, successions; both such and such, and just so many.

To a reasonable creature, the same action is both according
to nature, and according to reason.

members.why: What offers nothing to reason or to charity is beneath the reasonable faculty. A test for objects, not a description of the work.
members.text:
What object soever, our reasonable and sociable faculty doth meet
with, that affords nothing either for the satisfaction of reason, or for
the practice of charity, she worthily doth think unworthy of herself.

In the whole constitution of man, I see not any virtue contrary
to justice, whereby it may be resisted and opposed. But one whereby
pleasure and voluptuousness may be resisted and opposed, I see:
continence.

As virtue and wickedness consist not in passion, but in action; so
neither doth the true good or evil of a reasonable charitable man
consist in passion, but in operation and action.

decisions: Treats the three lists as versions of one list. Marcus never says they are the same list.

Names the three places “other people, my body, my judgments”, and sums them up as “letting reason lead”. The names and the summary are the editor’s: 7.30 says reason commands the body and 7.8 that acting by reason is acting by nature; neither says it of other people or of judging.
Joins the passages about outcomes with those about obstacles in claim 5, as two sides of one point.

Inside the claims, three things rest on one passage each: that the common good comes first (7.30), that reason was made to command the body (7.30), and that proper work cannot harm (6.31).

seneca.becomes: With Seneca every claim gains a second author, the empty Practice label gets two exercises, “Why” gets a further argument, and “In action” gains what I may still prefer before a hardship comes. Nothing of Marcus’s is challenged.
seneca.statement: With Seneca the statement gains a preparation: I accept what happens, and I think ahead to it.

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: Such affairs come by order, and not by accident.
piece.follows: Troubles like these come by order, not by accident.
piece.context: Seneca has just listed his own illness, sick slaves and lost income; “such affairs” are those troubles, which he calls inevitable.
gives: is not chance

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: the very agencies which seem to bring harm are working for the preservation of the world
piece.follows: What seems to harm me is working to preserve the world.
piece.context: Seneca names the inner defence against Fortune: not chafing at what happens. “The very agencies” are the events that seem to harm us.
gives: It serves the whole

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: I have trained myself not merely to obey God, but to agree with His decisions
piece.follows: I can do more than obey what is decided: I can agree with it.
piece.context: Said of the times “when everything seems to go hard”; “His decisions” are the illness and losses of 96.1, which Seneca says are decreed.
gives: accept it, and more than accept it

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: It is to this law that our souls must adjust themselves, this they should follow, this they should obey. Whatever happens, assume that it was bound to happen, and do not be willing to rail at Nature.
piece.follows: My soul should adjust itself to nature’s law, take whatever happens as bound to happen, and not rail at it.
piece.context: “This law” is nature’s order of changing seasons and opposites, which we cannot alter; “it” is whatever that order brings.
gives: I shall accept it
fit myself to it

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: None of these things is unusual or unexpected.
piece.follows: Setbacks like these are neither unusual nor unexpected.
piece.context: “These things” are Lucilius’s slaves running away; Seneca widens it at once to every knock on life’s journey.
gives: None of it is unusual

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: whether Chance drives and tosses human affairs without method, philosophy ought to be our defence
piece.follows: Even if chance drives everything, philosophy is still my defence.
piece.context: Seneca answers the objection that philosophy is useless if fate, God or chance rules: in each case we need it. “Chance” is the third case.
gives: And if nothing governs the world

items.label: why
items.t: And refusing does not spare me: fate leads the willing and drags the unwilling.
items.why: Marcus argues from the good of the whole. This argues that I go either way. Marcus only touches it, in 12.11 (“why doest thou resist?”), which this article uses for something else. Seneca gives the line as Cleanthes’s, in his own Latin.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: the willing soul Fate leads, but the unwilling drags along
support.follows: Fate takes me along whether I am willing or not.
support.context: The last line of Cleanthes’s prayer to Jupiter, which Seneca puts into Latin to close a letter on following nature’s law; the soul is anyone’s.
gives: fate leads the willing and drags the unwilling

items.label: practice
items.t: I shall think ahead to everything that can happen, not only to what usually does, so that the blow is lighter when it comes.
items.why: The passages used here give no exercise. Seneca gives this one in three letters. He also warns against overdoing it: in Ep. 13.10 he says not to run out to meet a suffering that has not come.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: Our minds should be sent forward in advance to meet all problems, and we should consider, not what is wont to happen, but what can happen.
support.follows: I should think ahead to what can happen, not only to what usually happens.
support.context: Written after fire destroyed Lyons and shook his friend Liberalis; “all problems” are whatever Fortune can do, since the unexpected weighs heaviest.
gives: think ahead to everything that can happen, not only to what usually does

support.author: seneca
support.quote: If an evil has been pondered beforehand, the blow is gentle when it comes.
support.follows: A misfortune I have already thought about hits less hard.
support.context: Follows a picture of the man who hears of chains and exile calmly; “an evil” is any such threatened hardship, new only to the unprepared.
gives: the blow is lighter when it comes

support.author: seneca
support.quote: That which has been long expected comes more gently.
support.follows: What I have long expected is easier when it arrives.
support.context: The closing advice of a letter on illness: keep Fortune’s whole power before your eyes. “That which” is any blow she may strike.
gives: the blow is lighter when it comes

items.label: practice
items.t: For a set number of days I shall live on the plainest food and clothing, and ask myself: is this what I was afraid of?
items.why: A second exercise, done with the body and not only in thought. It rehearses a loss before it comes; that is how it bears on accepting what happens.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: Set aside a certain number of days, during which you shall be content with the scantiest and cheapest fare, with coarse and rough dress, saying to yourself the while: “Is this the condition that I feared?”
support.follows: I should spend set days living poorly and ask myself whether this is what I feared.
support.context: A lesson for the Saturnalia: rehearse poverty while Fortune is kind, so that she cannot catch me off guard. “The condition” is being poor.

items.label: doubt
items.t: In that case my stance changes too: a god I follow gladly, but chance I endure, and defy.
items.why: Marcus says only that I can still govern myself. Seneca adds how to stand toward a world run by chance.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: She will encourage us to obey God cheerfully, but Fortune defiantly; she will teach us to follow God and endure Chance.
support.follows: Philosophy teaches me to obey a god cheerfully, and to endure chance and defy it.
support.context: “She” is philosophy, our defence whether fate, God or chance rules; the sentence sets how to stand toward God against how to stand toward Fortune.

items.label: action
items.t: I need not wish for the hardship. I may prefer to be spared it; what I want, if it must be borne, is to bear it with courage.
items.why: Marcus says to be glad of what comes; he does not say what I may wish beforehand. Seneca does. It is not a disagreement: Seneca too is pleased with what has come (Ep. 96.2, 74.20).

support.author: seneca
support.quote: I should prefer to be free from torture; but if the time comes when it must be endured, I shall desire that I may conduct myself therein with bravery, honour, and courage.
support.follows: I may prefer not to be tortured; if it must be endured, what I desire is to bear it with courage.
support.context: Lucilius asked whether brave endurance of torture is a thing to pray for; Seneca answers that the bravery is desirable, not the torture.
gives: I may prefer to be spared it; what I want, if it must be borne, is to bear it with courage

support.author: seneca
support.quote: The conclusion is, not that hardships are desirable, but that virtue is desirable, which enables us patiently to endure hardships.
support.follows: Hardships are not what is desirable; the virtue that lets me endure them is.
support.context: The conclusion Seneca draws from torture, war and illness; “virtue” is brave conduct in them, the only thing there he calls desirable.
gives: I need not wish for the hardship

passages.title: On facing hardships
passages.text: Such affairs come by order, and not by accident. If you will believe me, it is my inmost emotions that I am just now disclosing to you: when everything seems to go hard and uphill, I have trained myself not merely to obey God, but to agree with His decisions. I follow Him because my soul wills it, and not because I must. Nothing will ever happen to me that I shall receive with ill humour or with a wry face. I shall pay up all my taxes willingly. Now all the things which cause us to groan or recoil, are part of the tax of life—things, my dear Lucilius, which you should never hope and never seek to escape.

passages.title: On virtue as a refuge from worldly distractions
passages.text: It is the ability to refrain from chafing over whatever happens to one, of knowing that the very agencies which seem to bring harm are working for the preservation of the world, and are a part of the scheme for bringing to fulfilment the order of the universe and its functions. Let man be pleased with whatever has pleased God; let him marvel at himself and his own resources for this very reason, that he cannot be overcome, that he has the very powers of evil subject to his control, and that he brings into subjection chance and pain and wrong by means of that strongest of powers—reason.

passages.title: On obedience to the universal will
passages.text: It is to this law that our souls must adjust themselves, this they should follow, this they should obey. Whatever happens, assume that it was bound to happen, and do not be willing to rail at Nature. That which you cannot reform, it is best to endure, and to attend uncomplainingly upon the God under whose guidance everything progresses; for it is a bad soldier who grumbles when following his commander.

passages.title: On obedience to the universal will
passages.text: None of these things is unusual or unexpected. It is as nonsensical to be put out by such events as to complain of being spattered in the street or at getting befouled in the mud. The programme of life is the same as that of a bathing establishment, a crowd, or a journey: sometimes things will be thrown at you, and sometimes they will strike you by accident. Life is not a dainty business. You have started on a long journey; you are bound to slip, collide, fall, become weary, and cry out: “O for Death!”—or in other words, tell lies. At one stage you will leave a comrade behind you, at another you will bury someone, at another you will be apprehensive. It is amid stumblings of this sort that you must travel out this rugged journey.

passages.title: On philosophy, the guide of life
passages.text: Whether the truth, Lucilius, lies in one or in all of these views, we must be philosophers; whether Fate binds us down by an inexorable law, or whether God as arbiter of the universe has arranged everything, or whether Chance drives and tosses human affairs without method, philosophy ought to be our defence. She will encourage us to obey God cheerfully, but Fortune defiantly; she will teach us to follow God and endure Chance.

passages.title: On obedience to the universal will
passages.text: Lead me, O Master of the lofty heavens, My Father, whithersoever thou shalt wish. I shall not falter, but obey with speed. And though I would not, I shall go, and suffer, In sin and sorrow what I might have done In noble virtue. Aye, the willing soul Fate leads, but the unwilling drags along.

passages.title: On the lesson to be drawn from the burning of lyons [ 1 ]
passages.text: Therefore, nothing ought to be unexpected by us. Our minds should be sent forward in advance to meet all problems, and we should consider, not what is wont to happen, but what can happen. For what is there in existence that Fortune, when she has so willed, does not drag down from the very height of its prosperity? And what is there that she does not the more violently assail the more brilliantly it shines? What is laborious or difficult for her?

passages.title: On learning wisdom in old age
passages.text: If an evil has been pondered beforehand, the blow is gentle when it comes. To the fool, however, and to him who trusts in fortune, each event as it arrives “comes in a new and sudden form,” and a large part of evil, to the inexperienced, consists in its novelty. This is proved by the fact that men endure with greater courage, when they have once become accustomed to them, the things which they had at first regarded as hardships.

passages.title: On the healing power of the mind
passages.text: Meanwhile, hold fast to this thought, and grip it close: yield not to adversity; trust not to prosperity; keep before your eyes the full scope of Fortune’s power, as if she would surely do whatever is in her power to do. That which has been long expected comes more gently. Farewell.

passages.title: On festivals and fasting
passages.text: I am so firmly determined, however, to test the constancy of your mind that, drawing from the teachings of great men, I shall give you also a lesson: Set aside a certain number of days, during which you shall be content with the scantiest and cheapest fare, with coarse and rough dress, saying to yourself the while: “Is this the condition that I feared?”

passages.title: On ill-health and endurance of suffering
passages.text: My dear Lucilius, you must distinguish between these cases; you will then comprehend that there is something in them that is to be desired. I should prefer to be free from torture; but if the time comes when it must be endured, I shall desire that I may conduct myself therein with bravery, honour, and courage. Of course I prefer that war should not occur; but if war does occur, I shall desire that I may nobly endure the wounds, the starvation, and all that the exigency of war brings. Nor am I so mad as to crave illness; but if I must suffer illness, I shall desire that I may do nothing which shows lack of restraint, and nothing that is unmanly. The conclusion is, not that hardships are desirable, but that virtue is desirable, which enables us patiently to endure hardships.

claims.role: It comes from one chain of causes
claims.t: What happens to me is not chance. All things are linked together, and it comes from a chain of causes, the same that produced me.
claims.shared: Five passages use one family of words: connection, concatenation, coherence, linked, correspondence. Two (7.6, 4.36) say that things hold together. Three (10.5, 5.8, 1.17) say that what happens comes through that holding. Only 10.5 says the same causes produced me, and only 1.17 speaks of chance.
claims.changed: “Not a random blow from outside” is gone: no passage says “from outside”, and 4.36 sets its order against a bare sequence, not against chance. 7.6 now backs “linked together”, which it says, and no longer “chain of causes”, which it does not.

For by the same coherence of causes, by
which thy substance from all eternity was appointed to be, was also
whatsoever should happen unto it, destinated and appointed.
support.follows: The causes that produced me also produced everything that happens to me.
gives: it comes from a chain of causes
the same that produced me

support.quote:
from the very beginning by the series
and connection of the first causes, it hath ever had a reference unto
thee
support.follows: What happens to me was connected to me from the beginning through the chain of causes.

support.quote:
All things are linked and knitted

those

There
is then to be seen in the things of the world, not a bare succession,

support.follows: The things of the world do not merely follow one another; they correspond and belong together.

claims.t: It serves the whole of which I am a part. What serves the whole is good for every part, and a part has no reason to complain of it.
claims.shared: Three passages say that what happens is useful to the whole, and two that I am a part of it. Two go on to the part, and each says a different thing: 1.17 that what the whole needs is good for every part, 9.38 that a part has no reason to complain of it. They share the subject, not the conclusion.
claims.changed: Was “what serves the whole is not bad for the part”, a middle wording that neither passage says: 1.17 says “good”, and 9.38 speaks of complaining, not of harm. Each now backs its own words.

Whatsoever in any kind doth happen to any one, is expedient to the
whole.
support.follows: What happens to any individual is useful to the whole.
gives: It serves the whole

support.quote:
For this whatsoever it be, should not have been produced,
had it not conduced to the good of the universe.
support.follows: Nothing would have happened unless it helped the good of the universe.
gives: It serves the whole

support.quote:
whatsoever it is that is, is both

whatsoever it is that is requisite and necessary for the preservation of
the general, must of necessity for every particular nature, be good and

support.follows: Whatever is needed to preserve the whole is good and useful for every part of it.
gives: What serves the whole is good for every part

all things by the providence of reason happen unto every
particular, as a part of one general body; and then it is against reason

support.follows: If things happen to each of us as a part of one body, a part has no reason to complain of what happens for the good of the whole.

claims.t: So I shall accept it, and more than accept it: fit myself to it and be glad of it, as I take a harsh prescription for the sake of health.

Fit and accommodate thyself to that estate and to those

to like and

therefore entire and perfect) is maimed, and mutilated, if thou shalt
