members.text:
Up and down, from one age to another, go the ordinary things of
the world; being still the same. And either of everything in particular
before it come to pass, the mind of the universe doth consider with
itself and deliberate: and if so, then submit for shame unto the
determination of such an excellent understanding: or once for all it did
resolve upon all things in general; and since that whatsoever happens,
happens by a necessary consequence, and all things indivisibly in a
manner and inseparably hold one of another. In sum, either there is a
God, and then all is well; or if all things go by chance and fortune,
yet mayest thou use thine own providence in those things that concern
thee properly; and then art thou well.

Let not things future trouble thee. For if necessity so require that
they come to pass, thou shalt (whensoever that is) be provided for them
with the same reason, by which whatsoever is now present, is made both
tolerable and acceptable unto thee. All things are linked and knitted
together, and the knot is sacred, neither is there anything in the
world, that is not kind and natural in regard of any other thing, or,
that hath not some kind of reference and natural correspondence with
whatsoever is in the world besides. For all things are ranked together,
and by that decency of its due place and order that each particular
doth observe, they all concur together to the making of one and the same
κόσμος or world: as if you said, a comely piece, or an orderly
composition. For all things throughout, there is but one and the same
order; and through all things, one and the same God, the same substance
and the same law. There is one common reason, and one common truth, that
belongs unto all reasonable creatures, for neither is there save one
perfection of all creatures that are of the same kind, and partakers of
the same reason.

As we say commonly, The physician hath prescribed unto this man,
riding; unto another, cold baths; unto a third, to go barefoot: so it
is alike to say, The nature of the universe hath prescribed unto this
man sickness, or blindness, or some loss, or damage or some such thing.
For as there, when we say of a physician, that he hath prescribed
anything, our meaning is, that he hath appointed this for that, as
subordinate and conducing to health: so here, whatsoever doth happen
unto any, is ordained unto him as a thing subordinate unto the fates,
and therefore do we say of such things, that they do συμβαίνειν, that
is, happen, or fall together; as of square stones, when either in
walls, or pyramids in a certain position they fit one another, and
agree as it were in an harmony, the masons say, that they do
συμβαίνειν; as if thou shouldest say, fall together: so that in the
general, though the things be divers that make it, yet the consent or
harmony itself is but one. And as the whole world is made up of all the
particular bodies of the world, one perfect and complete body, of the
same nature that particular bodies; so is the destiny of particular
causes and events one general one, of the same nature that particular
causes are. What I now say, even they that are mere idiots are not
ignorant of: for they say commonly τοῦτο ἔφερεν ἀυτῷ, that is, This
his destiny hath brought upon him. This therefore is by the fates
properly and particularly brought upon this, as that unto this in
particular is by the physician prescribed. These therefore let us
accept of in like manner, as we do those that are prescribed unto us
our physicians. For them also in themselves shall We find to contain
many harsh things, but we nevertheless, in hope of health, and
recovery, accept of them. Let the fulfilling and accomplishment of
those things which the common nature hath determined, be unto thee as
thy health. Accept then, and be pleased with whatsoever doth happen,
though otherwise harsh and un-pleasing, as tending to that end, to the
health and welfare of the universe, and to Jove's happiness and
prosperity. For this whatsoever it be, should not have been produced,
had it not conduced to the good of the universe. For neither doth any
ordinary particular nature bring anything to pass, that is not to
whatsoever is within the sphere of its own proper administration and
government agreeable and subordinate. For these two considerations then
thou must be well pleased with anything that doth happen unto thee.
First, because that for thee properly it was brought to pass, and unto
thee it was prescribed; and that from the very beginning by the series
and connection of the first causes, it hath ever had a reference unto
thee. And secondly, because the good success and perfect welfare, and
indeed the very continuance of Him, that is the Administrator of the
whole, doth in a manner depend on it. For the whole (because whole,
therefore entire and perfect) is maimed, and mutilated, if thou shalt
cut off anything at all, whereby the coherence, and contiguity as of
parts, so of causes, is maintained and preserved. Of which certain it
is, that thou doest (as much as lieth in thee) cut off, and in some
sort violently take somewhat away, as often as thou art displeased with
anything that happeneth.

Whatsoever proceeds from the gods immediately, that any man will
grant totally depends from their divine providence. As for those
things that are commonly said to happen by fortune, even those must be
conceived to have dependence from nature, or from that first and general
connection, and concatenation of all those things, which more apparently
by the divine providence are administered and brought to pass.
All things flow from thence: and whatsoever it is that is, is both
necessary, and conducing to the whole (part of which thou art), and
whatsoever it is that is requisite and necessary for the preservation of
the general, must of necessity for every particular nature, be good and
behoveful. And as for the whole, it is preserved, as by the perpetual
mutation and conversion of the simple elements one into another, so
also by the mutation, and alteration of things mixed and compounded. Let
these things suffice thee; let them be always unto thee, as thy general
rules and precepts. As for thy thirst after books, away with it with all
speed, that thou die not murmuring and complaining, but truly meek and
well satisfied, and from thy heart thankful unto the gods.

Fit and accommodate thyself to that estate and to those
occurrences, which by the destinies have been annexed unto thee; and
love those men whom thy fate it is to live with; but love them truly. An
instrument, a tool, an utensil, whatsoever it be, if it be fit for the
purpose it was made for, it is as it should be though he perchance that
made and fitted it, be out of sight and gone. But in things natural,
that power which hath framed and fitted them, is and abideth within them
still: for which reason she ought also the more to be respected, and we
are the more obliged (if we may live and pass our time according to her
purpose and intention) to think that all is well with us, and according
to our own minds. After this manner also, and in this respect it is,
that he that is all in all doth enjoy his happiness.

members.why: A list of reminders about order, death, pain and praise. Too many subjects to fuse with anything here.
members.text:
All things (saith he) are by certain order and appointment. And
what if the elements only.

It will suffice to remember, that all things in general are by certain
order and appointment: or if it be but few. And as concerning death,
that either dispersion, or the atoms, or annihilation, or extinction,
or translation will ensue. And as concerning pain, that that which is
intolerable is soon ended by death; and that which holds long must needs
be tolerable; and that the mind in the meantime (which is all in all)
may by way of interclusion, or interception, by stopping all manner of
commerce and sympathy with the body, still retain its own tranquillity.
Thy understanding is not made worse by it. As for those parts that
suffer, let them, if they can, declare their grief themselves. As for
praise and commendation, view their mind and understanding, what estate
they are in; what kind of things they fly, and what things they seek
after: and that as in the seaside, whatsoever was before to be seen,
is by the continual succession of new heaps of sand cast up one upon
another, soon hid and covered; so in this life, all former things by
those which immediately succeed.

members.why: Questions to ask of any impression, tracing each thing to God, fate or a neighbour. An exercise in examining impressions, nearer to judgment than to accepting what happens.
members.text:
What is this, that now my fancy is set upon? of what things doth
it consist? how long can it last? which of all the virtues is the proper
virtue for this present use? as whether meekness, fortitude, truth,
faith, sincerity, contentation, or any of the rest? Of everything
therefore thou must use thyself to say, This immediately comes from God,
this by that fatal connection, and concatenation of things, or (which
almost comes to one) by some coincidental casualty. And as for this, it
proceeds from my neighbour, my kinsman, my fellow: through his ignorance
indeed, because he knows not what is truly natural unto him: but I know
it, and therefore carry myself towards him according to the natural law
of fellowship; that is kindly, and justly. As for those things that of
themselves are altogether indifferent, as in my best judgment I conceive
everything to deserve more or less, so I carry myself towards it.

Whatsoever doth happen in the world, is, in the course of nature,
as usual and ordinary as a rose in the spring, and fruit in summer. Of
the same nature is sickness and death; slander, and lying in wait, and
whatsoever else ordinarily doth unto fools use to be occasion either
of joy or sorrow. That, whatsoever it is, that comes after, doth always
very naturally, and as it were familiarly, follow upon that which was
before. For thou must consider the things of the world, not as a loose
independent number, consisting merely of necessary events; but as a
discreet connection of things orderly and harmoniously disposed. There
is then to be seen in the things of the world, not a bare succession,
but an admirable correspondence and affinity.

Either fate, (and that either an absolute necessity, and unavoidable
decree; or a placable and flexible Providence) or all is a mere
casual confusion, void of all order and government. If an absolute and
unavoidable necessity, why doest thou resist? If a placable and exorable
Providence, make thyself worthy of the divine help and assistance. If
all be a mere confusion without any moderator, or governor, then hast
thou reason to congratulate thyself; that in such a general flood of
confusion thou thyself hast obtained a reasonable faculty, whereby thou
mayest govern thine own life and actions. But if thou beest carried
away with the flood, it must be thy body perchance, or thy life, or some
other thing that belongs unto them that is carried away: thy mind and
understanding cannot. Or should it be so, that the light of a candle
indeed is still bright and lightsome until it be put out: and should
truth, and righteousness, and temperance cease to shine in thee whilest
thou thyself hast any being?

If so be that the Gods have deliberated in particular of those
things that should happen unto me, I must stand to their deliberation,
as discrete and wise. For that a God should be an imprudent God, is a
thing hard even to conceive: and why should they resolve to do me hurt?
for what profit either unto them or the universe (which they specially
take care for) could arise from it? But if so be that they have not
deliberated of me in particular, certainly they have of the whole in
general, and those things which in consequence and coherence of this
general deliberation happen unto me in particular, I am bound to embrace
and accept of. But if so be that they have not deliberated at all (which
indeed is very irreligious for any man to believe: for then let us
neither sacrifice, nor pray, nor respect our oaths, neither let us any
more use any of those things, which we persuaded of the presence and
secret conversation of the Gods among us, daily use and practise:)
but, I say, if so be that they have not indeed either in general, or
particular deliberated of any of those things, that happen unto us
in this world; yet God be thanked, that of those things that
concern myself, it is lawful for me to deliberate myself, and all my
deliberation is but concerning that which may be to me most profitable.
Now that unto every one is most profitable, which is according to his
own constitution and nature. And my nature is, to be rational in all my
actions and as a good, and natural member of a city and commonwealth,
towards my fellow members ever to be sociably and kindly disposed and
affected. My city and country as I am Antoninus, is Rome; as a man, the
whole world. Those things therefore that are expedient and profitable to
those cities, are the only things that are good and expedient for me.

members.why: What happens, happens justly. A stronger claim than claim 2, and only this passage makes it.
members.text:
Whatsoever doth happen in the world, doth happen justly, and so if
thou dost well take heed, thou shalt find it. I say not only in right
order by a series of inevitable consequences, but according to justice
and as it were by way of equal distribution, according to the true worth
of everything. Continue then to take notice of it, as thou hast begun,
and whatsoever thou dost, do it not without this proviso, that it be a
thing of that nature that a good man (as the word good is properly
taken) may do it. This observe carefully in every action.

To be capable of fancies and imaginations, is common to man and
beast. To be violently drawn and moved by the lusts and desires of the
soul, is proper to wild beasts and monsters, such as Phalaris and Nero
were. To follow reason for ordinary duties and actions is common to them
also, who believe not that there be any gods, and for their advantage
would make no conscience to betray their own country; and who when once
the doors be shut upon them, dare do anything. If therefore all things
else be common to these likewise, it follows, that for a man to like and
embrace all things that happen and are destinated unto him, and not to
trouble and molest that spirit which is seated in the temple of his own
breast, with a multitude of vain fancies and imaginations, but to keep
him propitious and to obey him as a god, never either speaking anything
contrary to truth, or doing anything contrary to justice, is the only
true property of a good man. And such a one, though no man should
believe that he liveth as he doth, either sincerely and conscionably,
or cheerful and contentedly; yet is he neither with any man at all angry
for it, nor diverted by it from the way that leadeth to the end of his
life, through which a man must pass pure, ever ready to depart, and
willing of himself without any compulsion to fit and accommodate himself
to his proper lot and portion.

Either all things by the providence of reason happen unto every
particular, as a part of one general body; and then it is against reason
that a part should complain of anything that happens for the good of the
whole; or if, according to Epicurus, atoms be the cause of all things
and that life be nothing else but an accidentary confusion of things,
and death nothing else, but a mere dispersion and so of all other
things: what doest thou trouble thyself for?

Whatsoever it be that happens unto thee, it is that which from all
time was appointed unto thee. For by the same coherence of causes, by
which thy substance from all eternity was appointed to be, was also
whatsoever should happen unto it, destinated and appointed.

Whatsoever in any kind doth happen to any one, is expedient to the
whole. And thus much to content us might suffice, that it is expedient
for the whole in general. But yet this also shalt thou generally
perceive, if thou dost diligently take heed, that whatsoever doth happen
to any one man or men.... And now I am content that the word expedient,
should more generally be understood of those things which we otherwise
call middle things, or things indifferent; as health, wealth, and the
like.

decisions: Presents the section as one argument by cases. Marcus gives the cases in four passages and never the whole chain in one place.

Keeps apart the two things said about the part: 1.17 says what the whole needs is good for every part, 9.38 that a part has no reason to complain. An earlier draft merged them into “not bad for the part”, which neither says.

Records no editor’s inference. The one “so”, in the claim under In action, is Marcus’s own: 5.8 gives the chain of causes and the good of the whole as its two reasons for being pleased with what happens.
Says nothing about acting to change what can be changed. That is Article 2. Accepting what has happened is not an instruction to do nothing.
articles.limit: Claims 1 to 4 hold only in the first case. If you do not think the world is governed, the article reduces to claim 5, and Marcus would not object: he says so himself. That what serves the whole is good for me has one witness here (1.17); Article 6 returns to it from its own passages.

seneca.becomes: With Seneca, four of the five claims gain a second author, the empty “When it breaks” gets its first item, “In action” says what worship of the governing power is enough, and “Why” gains a limit: its care may miss one person.
seneca.statement: With Seneca the statement stands and gains what follows for worship: to imitate what orders the world, by being good, is enough.

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: all that you behold, that which comprises both god and man, is one
piece.follows: Everything there is, divine and human, is one.
piece.context: Seneca's short rule for how to treat other people; “all that you behold” is the universe, gods and men together, of which we are parts.
gives: The world is one thing

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: the divine reason also is set in supreme command over all things, and is itself subject to none
piece.follows: Divine reason commands everything and answers to nothing.
piece.context: Opening of a letter that ranks the parts of a person; the rational part rules there as “the divine reason” rules over all things.
gives: What governs it is reason

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: One who thinks that they are unwilling to do harm, is wrong; they cannot do harm.
piece.follows: The gods are not merely unwilling to do harm; they are unable to.
piece.context: On the right idea of the gods, which worship needs; “they” are the gods, whom the next section calls supreme commanders in the universe.
gives: It has no cause to do evil

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: even this reason which we possess is the same, because it is derived from the divine reason
piece.follows: The reason in us is the same as the divine reason, because it comes from it.
piece.context: Same opening of the letter; “this reason which we possess” is the rational part of the human soul, set beside the divine reason.
gives: of one kind with it

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: the latter is the only thing that is not referred back to another, but rather refers all things to itself
piece.follows: The rational part answers to nothing else in a person, and everything else is referred to it.
piece.context: Same opening: body serves soul and the soul's lower parts serve its primary part; “the latter” is the rational element of that part.
gives: it turns everything else to its use

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: the force which inheres in all the seeds of things, giving them the power to fashion each thing according to its kind
piece.follows: Wisdom studies the force inside the seeds of things, which gives them the power to shape each thing.
piece.context: A list of what wisdom studies, as against the crafts; “she” is wisdom going back to the beginnings of things, and “them” are the seeds.
gives: the power at work

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: they all hinge on one alone, and that will be the creative cause
piece.follows: All causes depend on one cause.
piece.context: Seneca rejects Plato's and Aristotle's lists of causes; “they” are those listed causes, and the “one” is the maker, which he has just called Reason.
gives: the one source of all things

items.label: action
items.t: To worship what governs the world, it is enough to imitate it: to be a good man.
items.why: Marcus says to honour what is most powerful in the world. Seneca says what counts as worship enough.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: Would you win over the gods? Then be a good man. Whoever imitates them, is worshipping them sufficiently.
support.follows: To win over the gods, be a good man; imitating them is worship enough.
support.context: On how the gods should be worshipped; “them” are the gods, just called supreme commanders in the universe who control all things.

items.label: breaks
items.t: It is weakness to struggle against the order of the universe and speak ill of it, and to want to reform the gods sooner than myself.
items.why: Marcus has no passage in this section on what failing looks like. Seneca describes it, at the close of a letter on accepting what happens.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: that man is a weakling and a degenerate who struggles and maligns the order of the universe and would rather reform the gods than reform himself
support.follows: It is a weak man who fights and slanders the order of the universe and would sooner reform the gods than himself.
support.context: Close of a letter on accepting what happens as Fate's law; “that man” is whoever fights events instead of giving himself over to Fate.

items.label: why
items.t: What governs the world guards the human race, though it is sometimes unmindful of one person.
items.why: Marcus's 7.44 says that if it cares for anything in particular, it is for those who reason. Seneca says the care is for humankind and may miss one person. The two do not disagree: Marcus speaks only of a possibility.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: acting as guardians of the human race, even though they are sometimes unmindful of the individual
support.follows: The gods guard humankind but are sometimes unmindful of one person.
support.context: On what a worshipper should know of the gods; “they” are the gods, who command the universe and, he adds next, neither give nor have evil.

amend.t: , and to imitate what orders the world, by being good, is worship enough

passages.title: On the usefulness of basic principles
passages.text: all that you behold, that which comprises both god and man, is one—we are the parts of one great body. Nature produced us related to one another, since she created us from the same source and to the same end. She engendered in us mutual affection, and made us prone to friendships. She established fairness and justice; according to her ruling, it is more wretched to commit than to suffer injury. Through her orders, let our hands be ready for all that needs to be helped.

passages.title: On the happy life [ 1 ]
passages.text: You and I will agree, I think, that outward things are sought for the satisfaction of the body, that the body is cherished out of regard for the soul, and that in the soul there are certain parts which minister to us, enabling us to move and to sustain life, bestowed upon us just for the sake of the primary part of us. In this primary part there is something irrational, and something rational. The former obeys the latter, while the latter is the only thing that is not referred back to another, but rather refers all things to itself. For the divine reason also is set in supreme command over all things, and is itself subject to none; and even this reason which we possess is the same, because it is derived from the divine reason.

passages.title: On the usefulness of basic principles
passages.text: And what reason have the gods for doing deeds of kindness? It is their nature. One who thinks that they are unwilling to do harm, is wrong; they cannot do harm. They cannot receive or inflict injury; for doing harm is in the same category as suffering harm. The universal nature, all-glorious and all-beautiful, has rendered incapable of inflicting ill those whom it has removed from the danger of ill.

passages.title: On the part played by philosophy in the progress of man
passages.text: Then she goes back to the beginnings of things, to the eternal Reason which was imparted to the whole, and to the force which inheres in all the seeds of things, giving them the power to fashion each thing according to its kind. Then wisdom begins to inquire about the soul, whence it comes, where it dwells, how long it abides, into how many divisions it falls. Finally, she has turned her attention from the corporeal to the incorporeal, and has closely examined truth and the marks whereby truth is known, inquiring next how that which is equivocal can be distinguished from the truth, whether in life or in language; for in both are elements of the false mingled with the true.

passages.title: On the first cause
passages.text: Now, however, I am searching for the first, the general cause; this must be simple, inasmuch as matter, too, is simple. Do we ask what cause is? It is surely Creative Reason,—in other words, God. For those elements to which you referred are not a great series of independent causes; they all hinge on one alone, and that will be the creative cause.

passages.title: On the usefulness of basic principles
passages.text: The first way to worship the gods is to believe in the gods; the next to acknowledge their majesty, to acknowledge their goodness without which there is no majesty. Also, to know that they are supreme commanders in the universe, controlling all things by their power and acting as guardians of the human race, even though they are sometimes unmindful of the individual. They neither give nor have evil but they do chasten and restrain certain persons and impose penalties, and sometimes punish by bestowing that which seems good outwardly. Would you win over the gods? Then be a good man. Whoever imitates them, is worshipping them sufficiently.

passages.title: On obedience to the universal will
passages.text: Let us live thus, and speak thus; let Fate find us ready and alert. Here is your great soul—the man who has given himself over to Fate; on the other hand, that man is a weakling and a degenerate who struggles and maligns the order of the universe and would rather reform the gods than reform himself. Farewell.

claims.t: The world is one thing, ordered throughout, and all things in it are bound to one another.
claims.shared: Three passages call the world one (one living substance, a union, “one and general”), two call it ordered, and two say that all things in it are tied together. 4.22 and 6.8 each put order as one of two cases.
claims.changed: 4.33 says more: that each thing helps to cause the others. The claim keeps what 4.22 also says, that all things are bound together; the causing is kept in the practice claim.

support.quote:
the world as being but one living
substance, and having but one soul
support.follows: The world is one living thing with one soul.
gives: The world is one thing

support.quote:
can at one time subsist, and coexist in that both one and
general, which we call the world
support.follows: Everything that happens can exist together in one world.
gives: The world is one thing

support.quote:
or it is an union consisting of order, and administered
by Providence
support.follows: The second possibility is that the world is a unity made of order and run by providence.
gives: The world is one thing
ordered throughout
support.note: The second of two cases. The first is under “said once”.

support.quote:
Either this world is a κόσμος or comely piece, because all
disposed and governed by certain order
support.follows: One possibility is that the world is a well-made whole, because all in it is arranged and governed by order.
gives: ordered throughout
support.note: The first of two cases. In the second he still calls the world a comely piece.

support.quote:
and by what manner of
connection and concatenation all things happen
support.follows: Everything that happens is linked to the rest, as in a chain.
gives: all things in it are bound to one another

support.quote:
and yet all through diffused, and by natural sympathy,
one to another united
support.follows: All things, though different, run through one another and are united by a natural sympathy.
gives: all things in it are bound to one another

claims.t: What governs it is reason, and everything that happens comes from it. It has no cause to do evil, it is for community, and even what is harmful follows from something good.
claims.shared: 6.1 and 5.24 both name a rational essence that governs the universe. 6.1, 6.33 and 7.44 all say that whatever happens comes from it. The last three points each rest on one passage.
claims.changed: 6.33 says “all hurtful things”; the claim no longer softens this to “what looks harmful”. 6.33 says “one beginning” and 7.44 “the nature of the universe”; the claim says “it” for both.

support.quote:
That rational essence that doth govern it,
hath in itself no cause to do evil.
support.follows: The reason that governs the world has no motive to do evil.
gives: It has no cause to do evil
What governs it is reason

support.quote:
That rational essence by which the universe is governed, is for
community and society
support.follows: The reason that governs the world aims at community.
gives: it is for community
What governs it is reason

support.quote:
And
all things are done and determined according to its will and prescript.
support.follows: Everything is done and settled as the governing reason wills.
gives: everything that happens comes from it

support.quote:
And all
things come from one beginning; either all severally and particularly
deliberated and resolved upon, by the general ruler and governor of all;
or all by necessary consequence.
support.follows: All things come from one beginning: each decided by the ruler of all, or following by necessity.
gives: everything that happens comes from it

support.quote:
whatsoever it is, that
is and happens in the world, is either but a consequent of that one and
first deliberation
support.follows: Whatever happens follows from the first deliberation of the universe, unless it is cared for in particular.
gives: everything that happens comes from it
support.note: The first of two cases. In the second the ruling part also takes thought for particular things.

support.quote:
and all hurtful things, are but (as the thorn and
the mire) the necessary consequences of goodly fair things
support.follows: Harmful things are necessary by-products of good and fair things.
gives: even what is harmful follows from something good

claims.role: The same thing rules in me
claims.t: What rules in me is of one kind with it. It moves itself, and it turns everything else to its use. What I find in myself I can expect in the whole.
claims.shared: 5.18 and 6.7 both name a part of me that rules. 4.22 and 6.23 both argue from what is in me to what is in the whole. Only 5.18 says the two are of one kind.
claims.changed: 4.22 speaks of order in me and 6.23 of many things happening in me at once; the claim says “what I find in myself” for both. 5.18 says “all other things”, so “in me” is gone from the claim.

support.quote:
and
is of one kind and nature with that which we now spake of
support.follows: What is chief in me is of one kind and nature with what was just spoken of: what governs the world.
gives: of one kind with it

support.quote:
For it is the
very same, which being in thee, turneth all other things to its own use,
and by whom also thy life is governed.
support.follows: What is chief in me is the very same thing: it turns all else to its use and governs my life.
gives: it turns everything else to its use
What rules in me

support.quote:
The rational commanding part, as it alone can stir up and turn
itself
support.follows: The ruling part of me is the only thing that moves and directs itself.
gives: It moves itself
What rules in me

support.quote:
For is it possible that in
thee there should be any beauty at all, and that in the whole world
there should be nothing but disorder and confusion?
support.follows: If there is order in me, there cannot be only disorder in the world.
gives: What I find in myself I can expect in the whole
support.note: A likeness used as an argument: from order in me to order in the whole.

support.quote:
Consider how many different things, whether they concern our
bodies, or our souls, in a moment of time come to pass in every one of
us, and so thou wilt not wonder
support.follows: So much happens in me at one moment that I need not wonder at the world holding all things at once.
gives: What I find in myself I can expect in the whole

claims.t: I shall make a habit of asking what causes each thing: the power at work in it, considered apart from its matter, and the one source of all things.
claims.shared: 4.33 and 10.26 both make it a standing habit (“ever consider”, “thou must use to behold”). 10.26, 9.23 and 4.33 all point at the cause and not the thing; 6.33 and 4.33 at the one origin.

support.quote:
These things therefore
that are so secretly and invisibly wrought and brought to pass, thou
must use to behold and contemplate
support.follows: I must make it my practice to look at what is brought about out of sight.
gives: I shall make a habit

support.quote: Ever consider and think upon
support.follows: This is something to consider and think about always.
gives: I shall make a habit

support.quote:
and not the things themselves only,
but the power also by which they are effected
support.follows: I should look at the power that produces things, and not only at the things.
gives: the power at work
what causes each thing

support.quote:
Go to the quality of the cause from which the effect doth
proceed.
support.follows: I should go to the cause an effect comes from, and ask what kind of cause it is.
gives: what causes each thing

support.quote:
and how all things that
are, concur in the cause of one another's being
support.follows: Everything that exists helps cause everything else.
gives: what causes each thing

support.quote:
Behold it by itself bare and naked, separated from all that is
material.
support.follows: I should consider a cause by itself, apart from the material it works on.
gives: considered apart from its matter

support.quote: but consider in thy mind the true fountain of all
support.follows: I should keep in mind the true source of everything.
gives: the one source of all things

support.quote:
are done by one general motion
as it were, and deliberation of that one soul
support.follows: All things are done by one movement and one deliberation of the world's one soul.
gives: the one source of all things

claims.t: Thinking of the world as governed makes me calm, and I can be patient and trust what governs it.
claims.shared: 7.44 and 6.8 end on the same effect: tranquillity in one, quiet and patience in the other. Only 6.8 adds trust.
claims.changed: 7.44 says “often thought upon”; 6.8 puts it as a condition, “if the latter be”. The claim keeps the thought and the calm, which both have.

support.quote:
This often thought upon, will much
conduce to thy tranquillity.
support.follows: Thinking about this often brings calm.
gives: Thinking of the world as governed makes me calm

support.follows: If the world is ordered and governed, my worship is not wasted, and I will be quiet, patient and trusting.

single.quote:
Honour that which is chiefest and most powerful in the world, and
that is it, which makes use of all things, and governs all things. So
also in thyself; honour that which is chiefest, and most powerful
single.label: An instruction
single.t: I shall honour what is chief and most powerful in the world, and in the same way what is chief in myself.
single.why: Only 5.18 says “honour”. It is the one place where the likeness becomes an instruction.
single.follows: I should honour what is most powerful in the world, and likewise what is most powerful in me.

single.quote: neither can anything be hurt by it
single.label: A strong claim
single.t: Nothing can be hurt by it.
single.why: Only 6.1 goes this far. It is kept apart so that the claim on what governs the world does not rest on it.
single.follows: Nothing can be harmed by the reason that governs the world.

single.quote:
if so be that this ruling rational part of the
world, takes any thought and care of things particular, they are surely
his reasonable and principal creatures, that are the proper object of
his particular care and providence
single.label: A condition
single.t: If it takes thought for anything in particular, it is for those who reason.
single.why: Only 7.44 speaks of care for particular beings, and only as a possibility. It stood in the claim on what governs the world without backing any of its words.
single.follows: If the governing reason cares for anything in particular, it cares for reasoning beings.

single.quote:
If the first, why should I desire to continue any longer
in this fortuit confusion and commixtion?
single.label: The other case
single.t: If the world were only confusion, why should I wish to stay in it?
single.why: Only here does Marcus say how the ungoverned case would feel. Article 3 carries his calmer answer.
single.follows: If the world were mere confusion, there would be no reason to want to remain in it.

members.text:
According to the nature of the universe all things particular are
determined, not according to any other nature, either about compassing
and containing; or within, dispersed and contained; or without,
depending. Either this universe is a mere confused mass, and an
intricate context of things, which shall in time be scattered and
dispersed again: or it is an union consisting of order, and administered
by Providence. If the first, why should I desire to continue any longer
in this fortuit confusion and commixtion? or why should I take care for
anything else, but that as soon as may be I may be earth again? And
why should I trouble myself any more whilst I seek to please the Gods?
Whatsoever I do, dispersion is my end, and will come upon me whether I
will or no. But if the latter be, then am not I religious in vain;
then will I be quiet and patient, and put my trust in Him, who is the
Governor of all.

The nature of the universe did once certainly before it was
created, whatsoever it hath done since, deliberate and so resolve upon
the creation of the world. Now since that time, whatsoever it is, that
is and happens in the world, is either but a consequent of that one and
first deliberation: or if so be that this ruling rational part of the
world, takes any thought and care of things particular, they are surely
his reasonable and principal creatures, that are the proper object of
his particular care and providence. This often thought upon, will much
conduce to thy tranquillity.

That rational essence by which the universe is governed, is for
community and society; and therefore hath it both made the things that
are worse, for the best, and hath allied and knit together those
which are best, as it were in an harmony. Seest thou not how it hath
sub-ordinated, and co-ordinated? and how it hath distributed unto
everything according to its worth? and those which have the pre-eminency
and superiority above all, hath it united together, into a mutual
consent and agreement.

The matter itself, of which the universe doth consist, is of itself
very tractable and pliable. That rational essence that doth govern it,
hath in itself no cause to do evil. It hath no evil in itself; neither
can it do anything that is evil: neither can anything be hurt by it. And
all things are done and determined according to its will and prescript.

Ever consider and think upon the world as being but one living
substance, and having but one soul, and how all things in the world, are
terminated into one sensitive power; and are done by one general motion
as it were, and deliberation of that one soul; and how all things that
are, concur in the cause of one another's being, and by what manner of
connection and concatenation all things happen.

Consider how many different things, whether they concern our
bodies, or our souls, in a moment of time come to pass in every one of
us, and so thou wilt not wonder if many more things or rather all things
that are done, can at one time subsist, and coexist in that both one and
general, which we call the world.

Either this world is a κόσμος or comely piece, because all
disposed and governed by certain order: or if it be a mixture, though
confused, yet still it is a comely piece. For is it possible that in
thee there should be any beauty at all, and that in the whole world
there should be nothing but disorder and confusion? and all things in it
too, by natural different properties one from another differenced and
distinguished; and yet all through diffused, and by natural sympathy,
one to another united, as they are?

Asia, Europe; what are they, but as corners of the whole world;
of which the whole sea, is but as one drop; and the great Mount Athos,
but as a clod, as all present time is but as one point of eternity. All,
petty things; all things that are soon altered, soon perished. And all
things come from one beginning; either all severally and particularly
deliberated and resolved upon, by the general ruler and governor of all;
or all by necessary consequence. So that the dreadful hiatus of a gaping
lion, and all poison, and all hurtful things, are but (as the thorn and
the mire) the necessary consequences of goodly fair things. Think not
of these therefore, as things contrary to those which thou dost much
honour, and respect; but consider in thy mind the true fountain of all.

Honour that which is chiefest and most powerful in the world, and
that is it, which makes use of all things, and governs all things. So
also in thyself; honour that which is chiefest, and most powerful; and
is of one kind and nature with that which we now spake of. For it is the
very same, which being in thee, turneth all other things to its own use,
and by whom also thy life is governed.

From man is the seed, that once cast into the womb man hath no
more to do with it. Another cause succeedeth, and undertakes the
work, and in time brings a child (that wonderful effect from such a
beginning!) to perfection. Again, man lets food down through his
throat; and that once down, he hath no more to do with it. Another
cause succeedeth and distributeth this food into the senses, and the
affections: into life, and into strength; and doth with it those other
many and marvellous things, that belong unto man. These things therefore
that are so secretly and invisibly wrought and brought to pass, thou
must use to behold and contemplate; and not the things themselves only,
but the power also by which they are effected; that thou mayst behold
it, though not with the eyes of the body, yet as plainly and visibly as
thou canst see and discern the outward efficient cause of the depression
and elevation of anything.

Go to the quality of the cause from which the effect doth
proceed. Behold it by itself bare and naked, separated from all that is
material. Then consider the utmost bounds of time that that cause, thus
and thus qualified, can subsist and abide.

The rational commanding part, as it alone can stir up and turn
itself; so it maketh both itself to be, and everything that happeneth,
to appear unto itself, as it will itself.

decisions: Reads four descriptions of the world as one claim, and four of what governs it as another.

Makes the likeness between the whole and myself the centre of the article. Only 5.18 says the two are of one kind; 4.22 and 6.23 argue from myself to the whole, so the statement says “alike” and no more.
Keeps “nothing can be hurt by it” out of the fused claim, and keeps the particular care of 7.44 apart as well: Marcus puts it as a condition.
Joins 7.44 and 6.8 on calm as a claim of its own, under “In action”.
articles.limit: All twelve passages are used. This is a belief about the universe and the least argued of the five. Only 5.18 says that my reason and the world's are of one kind; the statement claims a likeness and no more. If you do not hold it, Articles 1 and 2 still stand on what human beings share, and Article 3 keeps its last claim.

seneca.becomes: With Seneca, each claim gains a second author on one of its parts, and the article gains three things Marcus leaves out here: the answer to what I was made for, what failing at it looks like, and the joy that is left when pleasure is ruled out.
seneca.statement: With Seneca the statement stands and gains its missing step. Marcus asks what I was made for and does not answer in this section; Seneca says outright that it is reason brought to perfection.

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: In each thing that quality should be best for which the thing is brought into being and by which it is judged.
piece.follows: In each thing, the quality that should be best is the one the thing was brought into being for.
piece.context: Seneca is proving that the honourable is the only good. “That quality” is each thing’s own excellence: a vine’s yield, a stag’s speed, a dog’s scent.
gives: is made for something

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: this wisdom I have declared already to be, both the good of others, and also his own
piece.follows: Wisdom is the good of other people and also the wise man’s own.
piece.context: Seneca is showing that hardship cannot stop the wise man from acting. “This wisdom” is what he still practises then; “his own” means the wise man’s.
gives: its fruit is for them as well as for itself

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: none of the objects which vanish from our gaze and are re-absorbed into the world of things, from which they have come forth and are soon to come forth again, is annihilated
piece.follows: Nothing that vanishes is destroyed: it is taken back into the world it came from and will come out of it again.
piece.context: Seneca is arguing against the fear of death. The “objects” are whatever dies or disappears, which he says will return; he is not speaking of waste or flaws.
gives: she takes it back into herself

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: Let us cherish and love old age; for it is full of pleasure if one knows how to use it. Fruits are most welcome when almost over
piece.follows: Old age is full of pleasure for one who knows how to use it, as fruit is most welcome when it is almost over.
piece.context: Seneca has just scolded his decaying house, his gnarled trees and an old slave, and seen his own age in them. “It” is old age; the fruit is his comparison.
gives: it has something pleasing of its own

items.label: why
items.t: What is peculiar to me as a human being is reason. Reason brought to perfection is the good that nature designed me for at birth, and when I fulfil it I have reached my highest good.
items.why: Marcus asks in 8.17 what I was made for and rules out pleasure, but this section never gives the answer. Seneca gives it in so many words.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: What then is peculiar to man? Reason.
support.follows: What belongs to a human being alone is reason.
support.context: The same proof that the honourable is the only good. “Peculiar to man” means what a human being has and animals and plants do not.
gives: What is peculiar to me as a human being is reason

support.author: seneca
support.quote: It is soul, and reason brought to perfection in the soul.
support.follows: What is a person’s own is the soul, and reason brought to perfection in it.
support.context: Seneca is saying what to praise in a person: not his slaves, house or income, which are outside him. “It” is the property peculiar to a human being.
gives: Reason brought to perfection

support.author: seneca
support.quote: man’s highest good is attained, if he has fulfilled the good for which nature designed him at birth
support.follows: A person reaches the highest good by fulfilling the good that nature designed him for at birth.
support.context: The close of the same argument. “The good for which nature designed him” is the reason just named, brought to perfection in the soul.
gives: the good that nature designed me for at birth
when I fulfil it I have reached my highest good

items.label: action
items.t: I am not to go without gladness. Real joy is a stern matter, and I rejoice only in what comes from my own store.
items.why: Marcus rules out pleasure as what I was made for (8.17) and says of joy only that reason enjoys its own fruit (9.8). Seneca says what joy remains and where it comes from.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: I do not wish you ever to be deprived of gladness
support.follows: Seneca does not want his friend ever to be without gladness.
support.context: Seneca tells Lucilius to learn how to feel joy and denies he is taking pleasures from him. “Gladness” is the kind born inside a person, not a gift of chance.
gives: I am not to go without gladness

support.author: seneca
support.quote: Real joy, believe me, is a stern matter.
support.follows: Real joy is serious, not light.
support.context: “Real joy” is that of a person who can despise death, face poverty and curb his pleasures. Seneca sets it against laughter and a cheerful face.
gives: Real joy is a stern matter

support.author: seneca
support.quote: rejoice only in that which comes from your own store
support.follows: I should rejoice only in what comes from within myself.
support.context: Said after telling Lucilius to trample what glitters outwardly. “Your own store” is, in his next words, your very self, the best part of you.
gives: I rejoice only in what comes from my own store

items.label: breaks
items.t: I really live when many make use of me and I make use of myself. If I creep into a hole and grow torpid, I have died before I am dead; and if I go into hiding out of fear, I am living not for myself but for my belly, my sleep and my lust.
items.why: Marcus has no passage in this section on what failing looks like. Seneca describes it twice: the man who is of use to no one, and the man who hides out of fear.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: He really lives who is made use of by many; he really lives who makes use of himself.
support.follows: To be really alive is to be of use to many and to make use of oneself.
support.context: The letter attacks living for the belly. “He” is set against those who obey their appetites, some of whom Seneca has just counted among the dead.
gives: I really live when many make use of me and I make use of myself

support.author: seneca
support.quote: Those men, however, who creep into a hole and grow torpid are no better off in their homes than if they were in their tombs.
support.follows: People who hide away and go numb are no better off at home than in a tomb.
support.context: “Those men” are the opposite of the man of use to many: people who withdraw into sloth, in a letter about living for the belly.
gives: If I creep into a hole and grow torpid

support.author: seneca
support.quote: he has died before he is dead
support.follows: Such a man has died before his death.
support.context: “He” is the same torpid man. Seneca says his name may be carved on the lintel of his house as on a tomb.
gives: I have died before I am dead

support.author: seneca
support.quote: who through fear has taken to concealment
support.follows: The man in question has gone into hiding out of fear.
support.context: Seneca is at the villa of Vatia, who was famous only for his leisure, and separates leisure from hiding. “Who” is the man fled from affairs and from men.
gives: if I go into hiding out of fear

support.author: seneca
support.quote: this person is not living for himself; he is living for his belly, his sleep, and his lust
support.follows: A man who hides like that does not live for himself; he lives for his belly, his sleep and his lust.
support.context: “This person” is the man who has hidden from affairs and people out of fear and failed desires. It is not anyone at rest, nor anyone enjoying himself.
gives: I am living not for myself but for my belly, my sleep and my lust

passages.title: On learning wisdom in old age
passages.text: Everything is estimated by the standard of its own good. The vine is valued for its productiveness and the flavour of its wine, the stag for his speed. We ask, with regard to beasts of burden, how sturdy of back they are; for their only use is to bear burdens. If a dog is to find the trail of a wild beast, keenness of scent is of first importance; if to catch his quarry, swiftness of foot; if to attack and harry it, courage. In each thing that quality should be best for which the thing is brought into being and by which it is judged.

passages.title: On some vain syllogisms
passages.text: but the wise man is not harmed by poverty, or by pain, or by any other of life’s storms. For all his functions are not checked, but only those which pertain to others; he himself is always in action, and is greatest in performance at the very time when fortune has blocked his way. For then he is actually engaged in the business of wisdom; and this wisdom I have declared already to be, both the good of others, and also his own.

passages.title: On the value of retirement
passages.text: And yet, if you are possessed by so great a craving for a longer life, reflect that none of the objects which vanish from our gaze and are re-absorbed into the world of things, from which they have come forth and are soon to come forth again, is annihilated; they merely end their course and do not perish. And death, which we fear and shrink from, merely interrupts life, but does not steal it away; the time will return when we shall be restored to the light of day; and many men would object to this, were they not brought back in forgetfulness of the past.

passages.title: On old age
passages.text: I owe it to my country-place that my old age became apparent whithersoever I turned. Let us cherish and love old age; for it is full of pleasure if one knows how to use it. Fruits are most welcome when almost over; youth is most charming at its close; the last drink delights the toper,—the glass which souses him and puts the finishing touch on his drunkenness.

passages.title: On learning wisdom in old age
passages.text: What then is peculiar to man? Reason. When this is right and has reached perfection, man’s felicity is complete. Hence, if everything is praiseworthy and has arrived at the end intended by its nature, when it has brought its peculiar good to perfection, and if man’s peculiar good is reason; then, if a man has brought his reason to perfection, he is praiseworthy and has reached the end suited to his nature. This perfect reason is called virtue, and is likewise that which is honourable.

passages.title: On the god within us
passages.text: Praise the quality in him which cannot be given or snatched away, that which is the peculiar property of the man. Do you ask what this is? It is soul, and reason brought to perfection in the soul. For man is a reasoning animal. Therefore, man’s highest good is attained, if he has fulfilled the good for which nature designed him at birth.

passages.title: On the true joy which comes from philosophy
passages.text: Above all, my dear Lucilius, make this your business: learn how to feel joy. Do you think that I am now robbing you of many pleasures when I try to do away with the gifts of chance, when I counsel the avoidance of hope, the sweetest thing that gladdens our hearts? Quite the contrary; I do not wish you ever to be deprived of gladness. I would have it born in your house; and it is born there, if only it be inside of you. Other objects of cheer do not fill a man’s bosom; they merely smooth his brow and are inconstant,—unless perhaps you believe that he who laughs has joy. The very soul must be happy and confident, lifted above every circumstance.

passages.title: On the true joy which comes from philosophy
passages.text: Real joy, believe me, is a stern matter. Can one, do you think, despise death with a care-free countenance, or with a “blithe and gay” expression, as our young dandies are accustomed to say? Or can one thus open his door to poverty, or hold the curb on his pleasures, or contemplate the endurance of pain? He who ponders these things in his heart is indeed full of joy; but it is not a cheerful joy. It is just this joy, however, of which I would have you become the owner; for it will never fail you when once you have found its source.

passages.title: On the true joy which comes from philosophy
passages.text: Therefore I pray you, my dearest Lucilius, do the one thing that can render you really happy: cast aside and trample under foot all those things that glitter outwardly and are held out to you by another or as obtainable from another; look toward the true good, and rejoice only in that which comes from your own store. And what do I mean by “from your own store”? I mean from your very self, that which is the best part of you. The frail body, also, even though we can accomplish nothing without it, is to be regarded as necessary rather than as important; it involves us in vain pleasures, short-lived, and soon to be regretted, which, unless they are reined in by extreme self-control, will be transformed into the opposite. This is what I mean: pleasure, unless it has been kept within bounds, tends to rush headlong into the abyss of sorrow. But it is hard to keep within bounds in that which you believe to be good. The real good may be coveted with safety.

passages.title: On harmful prayers
passages.text: Therefore those who, as Sallust puts it, “hearken to their bellies,” should be numbered among the animals, and not among men; and certain men, indeed, should be numbered, not even among the animals, but among the dead. He really lives who is made use of by many; he really lives who makes use of himself. Those men, however, who creep into a hole and grow torpid are no better off in their homes than if they were in their tombs. Right there on the marble lintel of the house of such a man you may inscribe his name, for he has died before he is dead. Farewell.

passages.title: On vatia’s villa
passages.text: For the man who has fled from affairs and from men, who has been banished to seclusion by the unhappiness which his own desires have brought upon him, who cannot see his neighbour more happy than himself, who through fear has taken to concealment, like a frightened and sluggish animal,—this person is not living for himself; he is living for his belly, his sleep, and his lust,—and that is the most shameful thing in the world. He who lives for no one does not necessarily live for himself. Nevertheless, there is so much in steadfastness and adherence to one’s purpose that even sluggishness, if stubbornly maintained, assumes an air of authority with us.

claims.t: Everything that exists, the gods included, is made for something and bears fruit of its own kind in its own time.
claims.shared: Both passages speak of everything, and both name the gods. What they say of it differs: 8.17 says it is made for something, 9.8 says it bears fruit of its kind, in its time.
claims.changed: “Made for something” and “bears fruit” are kept as two phrases, each from its own passage. Drops the horse, the vine and the sun as examples.

support.follows: Everything that exists was made for something, as a horse or a vine is.

is made for something

The sun itself will say of itself, I was made for
something; and so hath every god its proper function.

is made for something

claims.t: I was not made to please myself, but to keep exercising reason and fellowship. Reason by its nature turns toward other people, and its fruit is for them as well as for itself.
claims.shared: Two passages say that reason is by nature not a private thing: 6.13 calls the reasonable soul “naturally sociable”, 9.8 says reason is “of a diffusive nature” and begets itself in others. The rest is one passage each: 8.17 rules out pleasure, 6.13 names the exercise, 9.8 the fruit.
claims.changed: 8.17 only asks what I was made for and rules out pleasure. The “but” that answers it is the editor’s, and is marked.

inferences.why: 8.17 asks what I was made for and rules out only pleasure. The answer is the editor’s, taken from 6.13 and 9.8, which do not say “made for”.

support.quote:
What then were
then made for? to disport and delight thyself?
support.follows: I should ask what I was made for, and whether it can be to amuse and please myself.
gives: not made to please myself
support.note: Casaubon’s text reads “were then”. The question is put to the reader.

support.quote:
See how even common sense
and reason cannot brook it.
support.follows: Common sense and reason cannot accept that answer.
gives: not made to please myself

support.quote:
is careful to preserve his own, in the continual habit and
exercise both of reason and sociableness
support.follows: Such a person takes care to keep his own soul in the constant exercise of reason and fellowship.
gives: to keep exercising reason and fellowship

support.quote:
he that honours a reasonable soul in general, as it is reasonable and
naturally sociable
support.follows: What is to be honoured in a soul is that it is reasonable and, by nature, sociable.
gives: Reason by its nature turns toward other people

support.quote:
Reason is of a diffusive nature, what itself is in itself, it
begets in others, and so doth multiply.
support.follows: Reason spreads by nature: what it is in itself it produces in others, and so it multiplies.
gives: Reason by its nature turns toward other people

support.quote:
As for reason, that beareth both
common fruit for the use of others; and peculiar, which itself doth
enjoy.
support.follows: Reason produces something for others to use and something of its own that it enjoys.
gives: its fruit is for them as well as for itself

claims.t: What looks rotten or old to me looks different to someone who knows nature well. Nature throws nothing away: she takes it back into herself and makes new things out of it, and it has something pleasing of its own.
claims.shared: Both passages speak of the rotten and the old, and both appeal to the person acquainted with nature, who sees them differently: in 8.48 he laughs at the complaint, in 3.2 he alone finds the beauty. What he sees differs: 8.48 says nature reuses such things, 3.2 says they are pleasing as they are.
claims.changed: Drops “by-products” as the common term: 8.48 has shavings and 3.2 has “accessories”, but only as comparisons. The claim now rests on the two things both passages say outright.

support.quote:
whatsoever is within her
that seems either corrupted, or old, or unprofitable, she can change it
into herself, and of these very things can make new things
support.follows: What seems spoiled, old or useless, nature changes into herself and makes into new things.
gives: What looks rotten or old
she takes it back into herself and makes new things out of it

support.quote:
one that is
acquainted with the mysteries of nature, will laugh at thee for it
support.follows: Someone who knows how nature works would laugh at the question of what such things are for.

support.quote:
but the
nature of the universe hath no such out-place
support.follows: Nature has nowhere outside itself to discard anything.
gives: Nature throws nothing away

support.quote:
So ripe olives, when

single.quote:
Is the cucumber bitter? set it away. Brambles are in the way?
avoid them. Let this suffice.
single.label: A practice
single.t: If the cucumber is bitter, I set it aside; if brambles are in the way, I go round them. That is enough.
single.why: Only 8.48 gives the practice. Its second half is the next item.
single.follows: I should set the bitter thing aside, go round the obstacle, and leave it at that.

single.quote:
Add not presently speaking unto thyself,
What serve these things for in the world?
single.label: A prohibition
single.t: I do not ask of a bitter thing what it is for.
single.why: Only 8.48 forbids the question. Its reason is under “If I doubt it”: nature throws nothing away. Marcus does not say how this fits with 8.17, where everything was made for something.
single.follows: I should not go on to ask what such things are for.

single.quote:
in matter of
purposes and actions, we must presently see what is the proper use and
relation of every one
single.label: A practice
single.t: Of each purpose and each action, taken one at a time, I see at once what its proper use is.
single.why: Only 7.4 asks about use action by action. It speaks of what is said and done, not of what each thing is made for, so it backs no claim.
single.follows: For every purpose and action, I should see at once what its proper use is.

members.text:
This also thou must observe, that whatsoever it is that naturally
doth happen to things natural, hath somewhat in itself that is pleasing
and delightful: as a great loaf when it is baked, some parts of it
cleave as it were, and part asunder, and make the crust of it rugged and
unequal, and yet those parts of it, though in some sort it be against
the art and intention of baking itself, that they are thus cleft and
parted, which should have been and were first made all even and uniform,
they become it well nevertheless, and have a certain peculiar property,
to stir the appetite. So figs are accounted fairest and ripest then,
when they begin to shrink, and wither as it were. So ripe olives, when
they are next to putrefaction, then are they in their proper beauty. The
hanging down of grapes--the brow of a lion, the froth of a foaming wild
boar, and many other like things, though by themselves considered, they
are far from any beauty, yet because they happen naturally, they both
are comely, and delightful; so that if a man shall with a profound mind
and apprehension, consider all things in the world, even among all those
things which are but mere accessories and natural appendices as it were,
there will scarce appear anything unto him, wherein he will not find
matter of pleasure and delight. So will he behold with as much pleasure
the true _rictus_ of wild beasts, as those which by skilful painters and
other artificers are imitated. So will he be able to perceive the proper
ripeness and beauty of old age, whether in man or woman: and whatsoever
else it is that is beautiful and alluring in whatsoever is, with chaste
and continent eyes he will soon find out and discern. Those and many
other things will he discern, not credible unto every one, but unto them
only who are truly and familiarly acquainted, both with nature itself,
and all natural things.

Those things which the common sort of people do admire, are most
of them such things as are very general, and may be comprehended under
things merely natural, or naturally affected and qualified: as stones,
wood, figs, vines, olives. Those that be admired by them that are more
moderate and restrained, are comprehended under things animated: as
flocks and herds. Those that are yet more gentle and curious, their
admiration is commonly confined to reasonable creatures only; not in
general as they are reasonable, but as they are capable of art, or of
some craft and subtile invention: or perchance barely to reasonable
creatures; as they that delight in the possession of many slaves. But
he that honours a reasonable soul in general, as it is reasonable and
naturally sociable, doth little regard anything else: and above all
things is careful to preserve his own, in the continual habit and
exercise both of reason and sociableness: and thereby doth co-operate
with him, of whose nature he doth also participate; God.

Whatsoever is, was made for something: as a horse, a vine. Why
wonderest thou? The sun itself will say of itself, I was made for
something; and so hath every god its proper function. What then were
then made for? to disport and delight thyself? See how even common sense
and reason cannot brook it.

Is the cucumber bitter? set it away. Brambles are in the way?
avoid them. Let this suffice. Add not presently speaking unto thyself,
What serve these things for in the world? For, this, one that is
acquainted with the mysteries of nature, will laugh at thee for it; as a
carpenter would or a shoemaker, if meeting in either of their shops with
some shavings, or small remnants of their work, thou shouldest blame
them for it. And yet those men, it is not for want of a place where to
throw them that they keep them in their shops for a while: but the
nature of the universe hath no such out-place; but herein doth consist
the wonder of her art and skill, that she having once circumscribed
herself within some certain bounds and limits, whatsoever is within her
that seems either corrupted, or old, or unprofitable, she can change it
into herself, and of these very things can make new things; so that she
needeth not to seek elsewhere out of herself either for a new supply of
matter and substance, or for a place where to throw out whatsoever is
irrecoverably putrid and corrupt. Thus she, as for place, so for matter
and art, is herself sufficient unto herself.

Man, God, the world, every one in their kind, bear some fruits.
All things have their proper time to bear. Though by custom, the word
itself is in a manner become proper unto the vine, and the like, yet is
it so nevertheless, as we have said. As for reason, that beareth both
common fruit for the use of others; and peculiar, which itself doth
enjoy. Reason is of a diffusive nature, what itself is in itself, it
begets in others, and so doth multiply.

Word after word, every one by itself, must the things that are
spoken be conceived and understood; and so the things that are done,
purpose after purpose, every one by itself likewise. And as in matter of
purposes and actions, we must presently see what is the proper use and
relation of every one; so of words must we be as ready, to consider of
every one what is the true meaning, and signification of it according to
truth and nature, however it be taken in common use.

members.why: What tragedy and comedy were instituted for. Purpose applied to drama, with nothing for a rule of life.
members.text:
Tragedies were at first brought in and instituted, to put men in mind
of worldly chances and casualties: that these things in the ordinary
course of nature did so happen: that men that were much pleased and
delighted by such accidents upon this stage, would not by the same
things in a greater stage be grieved and afflicted: for here you see
what is the end of all such things; and that even they that cry out
so mournfully to Cithaeron, must bear them for all their cries and
exclamations, as well as others. And in very truth many good things are
spoken by these poets; as that (for example) is an excellent passage:
'But if so be that I and my two children be neglected by the Gods, they
have some reason even for that,' &c. And again, 'It will but little
avail thee to storm and rage against the things themselves,' &c. Again,
'To reap one's life, as a ripe ear of corn;' and whatsoever else is
to be found in them, that is of the same kind. After the tragedy, the
ancient comedy was brought in, which had the liberty to inveigh against
personal vices; being therefore through this her freedom and liberty
of speech of very good use and effect, to restrain men from pride
and arrogancy. To which end it was, that Diogenes took also the same
liberty. After these, what were either the Middle, or New Comedy
admitted for, but merely, (Or for the most part at least) for the
delight and pleasure of curious and excellent imitation? 'It will steal
away; look to it,' &c. Why, no man denies, but that these also have some
good things whereof that may be one: but the whole drift and foundation
of that kind of dramatical poetry, what is it else, but as we have said?

decisions: Uses 6.13 and 9.8 to answer the question that 8.17 asks and leaves open. The step is marked as the editor’s: “namely” in the statement, “but” in claim 2.
Fuses 8.17 with 9.8 only on what both say: the rule covers everything, the gods included. “Made for something” is 8.17’s and “bears fruit” is 9.8’s, and the claim keeps them apart.
Fuses 6.13 with 9.8 on reason turning by its nature toward other people (“naturally sociable”, “of a diffusive nature”).
Fuses 8.48 with 3.2, the most central passage of the section, on the rotten and the old and on the person who knows nature. That nature reuses them is 8.48 alone; that they are pleasing is 3.2 alone.
Keeps 7.4 as a said-once practice. It was a witness to claim 1 without backing any of its words.
8.17 says everything was made for something; 8.48 forbids asking what a bitter thing is for. Neither passage mentions the other, and the article keeps both without reconciling them.
articles.limit: This is the smallest and loosest section: seven passages, six used. Claims 1 and 3 rest on two passages and claim 2 on three, and in each claim only part of the sentence is said by two passages: the scope in claim 1, reason’s turn toward others in claim 2, the rotten and the old and the person who knows nature in claim 3. The rest of each claim is one passage’s. That what I was made for is reason is the editor’s step; no passage of this section says it.
