seneca.becomes: With Seneca, taking the universe’s side gains two witnesses, and the article gains what Marcus leaves out here: the hard things, paid willingly as a tax; words for a setback; a test for prayer; how to stand under pain; an answer when a death seems too early; and what holds if I doubt it. He backs nothing in the first claim, and he limits the second: he does not crave hardship itself.
seneca.statement: With Seneca the statement stands and takes in the hard things: I take the whole’s side, and what is hard in what it brings I pay willingly, as a tax on being alive. He does not say that I should want it.

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: I have trained myself not merely to obey God, but to agree with His decisions
piece.follows: Seneca has trained himself to agree with what God decides, and not only to obey it.
piece.context: Seneca answers a complaining Lucilius. “His decisions” are God’s: the illness and losses Seneca has just listed as his own, which he says come by order and not by accident.
gives: I take the universe’s side

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: Let man be pleased with whatever has pleased God
piece.follows: A person should be pleased with whatever has pleased God.
piece.context: On the inner defence against Fortune: not chafing at what happens to one. “Whatever has pleased God” is whatever happens, including what seems to bring harm.
gives: I take the universe’s side

items.label: action
items.t: The hard things are a tax on being alive, and I pay it willingly. Whatever makes me groan or shrink back is part of that tax, and I do not hope or try to escape it.
items.why: In this section Marcus calls what comes fruit and says it is timely; none of his passages names the hard part of it. Seneca names it, and calls it a tax, not a fruit. He says how to receive it: willingly. He does not say that I should want it.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: I shall pay up all my taxes willingly.
support.follows: Seneca will pay every tax he owes, and pay it willingly.
support.context: From Letter 96, where Seneca tells Lucilius to agree with what God decides. The “taxes” are not money: the next sentence says they are everything in life that makes us groan or recoil.
gives: I pay it willingly

support.author: seneca
support.quote: Now all the things which cause us to groan or recoil, are part of the tax of life—things, my dear Lucilius, which you should never hope and never seek to escape.
support.follows: What makes us groan or recoil is part of the price of living, and we should neither hope nor try to escape it.
support.context: Said to Lucilius, who had feared for his life in an illness. The things that make us groan are the illness, losses, toil and fear listed just before.
gives: The hard things are a tax on being alive
Whatever makes me groan or shrink back is part of that tax
I do not hope or try to escape it

items.label: practice
items.t: Whenever something turns out against what I expected, I say to myself: “Heaven decreed better.”
items.why: Marcus gives words to say of the world: “Dear city of Zeus”. Seneca gives words to say at each setback. They say that what was decided is better than what I expected; they do not say, as 10.21 does, that it is good for me.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: say to yourself, whenever things turn out contrary to your expectation: “Heaven decreed better!”
support.follows: When things go against what I expected, I should tell myself that the gods decided better.
support.context: On holding what Fortune gives without leaning on it. He first offers “Heaven decreed it otherwise” for every mishap, then this, as braver and nearer the truth.
gives: Whenever something turns out against what I expected
Heaven decreed better

items.label: practice
items.t: I speak with God as if other people were listening. The day I ask for nothing that I could not ask for openly, I am free of my desires.
items.why: 5.7 says to pray simply and like a free person, and gives no test. Seneca gives one, and ties it to freedom as well: whoever asks only for what he could ask for openly is free of his desires.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: Know that thou art freed from all desires when thou hast reached such a point that thou prayest to God for nothing except what thou canst pray for openly.
support.follows: A person is free of his desires once he prays only for what he could pray for openly.
support.context: Seneca has just told Lucilius to drop his old prayers and ask for a sound mind. The saying is Athenodorus’s; to pray “openly” is to ask only for what others may hear.
gives: The day I ask for nothing that I could not ask for openly, I am free of my desires

support.author: seneca
support.quote: Live among men as if God beheld you; speak with God as if men were listening
support.follows: I should live as if God saw me and speak with God as if people heard me.
support.context: Seneca’s own advice, drawn from that saying: people whisper to the gods the base wishes they hide from men. To “speak with God” is to pray.
gives: I speak with God as if other people were listening

items.label: breaks
items.t: In pain or illness, if I give way to my suffering, it beats me. It is like a wall falling toward me: if I hold my ground and push against it, it is forced back.
items.why: 8.54 is about an obstacle in my way: I do not force it and I do not fall. Seneca speaks of something else, pain and illness that press on me, and says to stand up to them. He resists suffering that has to be borne; he does not attack an obstacle, so the two do not conflict.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: if he once gives way, he will be vanquished; but if he strives against his sufferings, he will conquer.
support.follows: Whoever gives way to his sufferings is beaten; whoever strives against them wins.
support.context: A letter on bearing illness and pain, to Lucilius, who is ill; Seneca recalls his own sickness. “He” is anyone in the midst of troubles, striving against his sufferings.
gives: if I give way to my suffering, it beats me

support.author: seneca
support.quote: but if you hold your ground and make up your mind to push against it, it will be forced back.
support.follows: What leans on me is forced back if I hold my ground and push against it.
support.context: Same passage. “It” is a falling ruin that leans on you: Seneca’s image for pain, which presses harder on the one who backs away from it.
gives: if I hold my ground and push against it, it is forced back

items.label: breaks
items.role: When a death seems too early
items.t: When a death seems to come too early, I ask which is fairer: that I obey nature, or that nature obey me. How soon I leave a place I must leave anyway makes no difference, and a short life can be a perfect one.
items.why: The time is this article’s own point: nothing is too early or too late for me. Seneca meets it in one case only, a death that seems to come too soon, and his answer is not Marcus’s. He does not say the time was right; he says the length of a life does not decide whether it is complete.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: do you consider it fairer that you should obey Nature, or that Nature should obey you? And what difference does it make how soon you depart from a place which you must depart from sooner or later?
support.follows: Seneca asks which is fairer, that I obey nature or that nature obey me, and what difference it makes how soon I leave a place I must leave.
support.context: Lucilius mourned the philosopher Metronax as dead too soon; Seneca calls such complaints railing at Fate. The “place which you must depart from” is life.
gives: which is fairer: that I obey nature, or that nature obey me
How soon I leave a place I must leave anyway makes no difference

support.author: seneca
support.quote: Just as one of small stature can be a perfect man, so a life of small compass can be a perfect life.
support.follows: A short life can be a perfect life, as a small man can be a perfect man.
support.context: Same letter: a life is to be measured by what was done in it, not by how long it lasted. “A life of small compass” is a short life.
gives: a short life can be a perfect one

items.label: doubt
items.role: Even if it is a disaster
items.t: Even if what comes is a disaster, a loss or a wrong, it has no more power over my virtue than a cloud has over the sun: my virtue shines less brightly, but it is no smaller.
items.why: No passage of Marcus in this section asks what holds if what comes is not good for me. Seneca’s answer is that even a disaster cannot make virtue smaller. He uses the sun for it, as 8.54 uses a sunbeam for the mind.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: obstacles take nothing away from virtue; it is no smaller, but merely shines with less brilliancy.
support.follows: Obstacles take nothing away from virtue; it only shines less brightly.
support.context: Seneca argues that a good man is happy even under misfortune. “Obstacles” are what stands in virtue’s way as an object stands before the sun, which is no smaller for it.
gives: my virtue shines less brightly, but it is no smaller

support.author: seneca
support.quote: Disasters, therefore, and losses, and wrongs, have only the same power over virtue that a cloud has over the sun.
support.follows: Disasters, losses and wrongs have no more power over virtue than a cloud has over the sun.
support.context: The conclusion of that comparison: a cloud hides the sun and takes nothing from it. “Virtue” is the good man’s, which Seneca holds to be his whole good.
gives: Even if what comes is a disaster, a loss or a wrong
it has no more power over my virtue than a cloud has over the sun

items.t: Seneca stops short of Marcus’s word “love”. He agrees with what God decides and receives it without complaint (Ep. 96.2), but he says he is not so mad as to crave a hardship: what he wants is the virtue that bears it. This limits the claim and does not contradict it. He would rather be spared beforehand and agrees once it comes; and of his own death he says he should desire whatever circumstances demand (Ep. 61.3).

support.author: seneca
support.quote: Nor am I so mad as to crave illness; but if I must suffer illness, I shall desire that I may do nothing which shows lack of restraint, and nothing that is unmanly.
support.follows: Seneca does not want illness; if he must be ill, what he wants is to do nothing unrestrained or weak in it.
support.context: Lucilius asked whether every good is desirable, since bravery under torture is a good. Seneca separates the hardship, which he does not want, from his conduct in it.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: The conclusion is, not that hardships are desirable, but that virtue is desirable, which enables us patiently to endure hardships.
support.follows: What is desirable is not hardship but the virtue that lets us bear hardship patiently.
support.context: Seneca’s own summing-up of his answer to that question. The “hardships” are the torture, war and illness he has just named.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: Let us therefore so set our minds in order that we may desire whatever is demanded of us by circumstances
support.follows: I should bring my mind to want whatever circumstances require of me.
support.context: Seneca, now old, writes that dying well means dying gladly and that one should do nothing unwillingly. What circumstances demand is, above all, his death.

passages.title: On facing hardships
passages.text: Such affairs come by order, and not by accident. If you will believe me, it is my inmost emotions that I am just now disclosing to you: when everything seems to go hard and uphill, I have trained myself not merely to obey God, but to agree with His decisions. I follow Him because my soul wills it, and not because I must. Nothing will ever happen to me that I shall receive with ill humour or with a wry face. I shall pay up all my taxes willingly. Now all the things which cause us to groan or recoil, are part of the tax of life—things, my dear Lucilius, which you should never hope and never seek to escape.

passages.title: On virtue as a refuge from worldly distractions
passages.text: It is the ability to refrain from chafing over whatever happens to one, of knowing that the very agencies which seem to bring harm are working for the preservation of the world, and are a part of the scheme for bringing to fulfilment the order of the universe and its functions. Let man be pleased with whatever has pleased God; let him marvel at himself and his own resources for this very reason, that he cannot be overcome, that he has the very powers of evil subject to his control, and that he brings into subjection chance and pain and wrong by means of that strongest of powers—reason.

passages.title: On the fickleness of fortune
passages.text: Nay rather, to adopt a phrase which is braver and nearer the truth—one on which you may more safely prop your spirit—say to yourself, whenever things turn out contrary to your expectation: “Heaven decreed better!” If you are thus poised, nothing will affect you and a man will be thus poised if he reflects on the possible ups and downs in human affairs before he feels their force, and if he comes to regard children, or wife, or property, with the idea that he will not necessarily possess them always and that he will not be any more wretched just because he ceases to possess them.

passages.title: On living to oneself
passages.text: But I must, as is my custom, send a little gift along with this letter. It is a true saying which I have found in Athenodorus: “Know that thou art freed from all desires when thou hast reached such a point that thou prayest to God for nothing except what thou canst pray for openly.” But how foolish men are now! They whisper the basest of prayers to heaven; but if anyone listens, they are silent at once. That which they are unwilling for men to know, they communicate to God. Do you not think, then, that some such wholesome advice as this could be given you: “Live among men as if God beheld you; speak with God as if men were listening”? Farewell.

passages.title: On the healing power of the mind
passages.text: But when set in the very midst of troubles one should say: Perchance some day the memory of this sorrow Will even bring delight. Let such a man fight against them with all his might: if he once gives way, he will be vanquished; but if he strives against his sufferings, he will conquer. As it is, however, what most men do is to drag down upon their own heads a falling ruin which they ought to try to support. If you begin to withdraw your support from that which thrusts toward you and totters and is ready to plunge, it will follow you and lean more heavily upon you; but if you hold your ground and make up your mind to push against it, it will be forced back.

passages.title: The epistles of seneca
passages.text: But tell me, pray, do you consider it fairer that you should obey Nature, or that Nature should obey you? And what difference does it make how soon you depart from a place which you must depart from sooner or later? We should strive, not to live long, but to live rightly; for to achieve long life you have need of Fate only, but for right living you need the soul. A life is really long if it is a full life; but fulness is not attained until the soul has rendered to itself its proper Good, that is, until it has assumed control over itself.

passages.title: The epistles of seneca
passages.text: Just as one of small stature can be a perfect man, so a life of small compass can be a perfect life. Age ranks among the external things. How long I am to exist is not mine to decide, but how long I shall go on existing in my present way is in my own control. This is the only thing you have the right to require of me,—that I shall cease to measure out an inglorious age as it were in darkness, and devote myself to living instead of being carried along past life.

passages.title: On the happy life [ 1 ]
passages.text: Similarly, obstacles take nothing away from virtue; it is no smaller, but merely shines with less brilliancy. In our eyes, it may perhaps be less visible and less luminous than before; but as regards itself it is the same and, like the sun when he is eclipsed, is still, though in secret, putting forth its strength. Disasters, therefore, and losses, and wrongs, have only the same power over virtue that a cloud has over the sun.

passages.title: On ill-health and endurance of suffering
passages.text: My dear Lucilius, you must distinguish between these cases; you will then comprehend that there is something in them that is to be desired. I should prefer to be free from torture; but if the time comes when it must be endured, I shall desire that I may conduct myself therein with bravery, honour, and courage. Of course I prefer that war should not occur; but if war does occur, I shall desire that I may nobly endure the wounds, the starvation, and all that the exigency of war brings. Nor am I so mad as to crave illness; but if I must suffer illness, I shall desire that I may do nothing which shows lack of restraint, and nothing that is unmanly. The conclusion is, not that hardships are desirable, but that virtue is desirable, which enables us patiently to endure hardships.

passages.title: On meeting death cheerfully
passages.text: That which is bound to be a necessity if you rebel, is not a necessity if you desire it. This is what I mean: he who takes his orders gladly, escapes the bitterest part of slavery,—doing what one does not want to do. The man who does something under orders is not unhappy; he is unhappy who does something against his will. Let us therefore so set our minds in order that we may desire whatever is demanded of us by circumstances, and above all that we may reflect upon our end without sadness.

claims.role: What comes is good, and on time
claims.t: What the whole brings me is good for me, and it comes at the right time: nothing that is timely for the whole is too early or too late for me.
claims.shared: Both passages say that what nature brings is good for the one it is brought to (10.21: “good for each”; 4.19: “fruit to me”). Both add the time: 10.21 that it is good when nature brings it, 4.19 that what is timely for the universe is never too early or too late for me.
claims.changed: 10.21 says “each”; the claim says “me”, as 4.19 does. 4.19 speaks to the universe and to nature as “you”; the claim speaks about them and calls both “the whole”, 10.21’s word.

single.quote: Surely the sun does not think it should do the rain’s part? Or Asclepius the part of the fruit-bearing goddess? And what of each of the stars? Are they not different, yet working together toward the same thing?
single.label: Different parts, one work
single.t: The sun does not do the rain’s part, and no god does another’s. The parts of the world differ, and they work together toward the same thing.
single.why: Only this passage speaks of the parts of the world and their separate tasks. No second passage of the section says it, so it is not fused.
single.follows: Each power keeps to its own part; the parts differ and work together toward the same thing.

single.quote: All things from you, all things in you, all things into you.
single.label: One source
single.t: Everything is from nature, in nature, and goes into nature.
single.why: Only this passage says it. It names a source, a place and a destination; it does not say that things work toward an end.
single.follows: All things are from nature, in nature and go into nature.

single.quote: One man says, “Dear city of Cecrops.” But you, will you not say, “Dear city of Zeus”?
single.label: A practice
single.t: As one man says “Dear city of Cecrops” of Athens, I say “Dear city of Zeus”.
single.why: Only this passage gives words to say. They are kept as the article’s practice.
single.follows: If one man can call Athens dear, I am asked to say “Dear city of Zeus”.

single.quote: A prayer of the Athenians: “Rain, rain, dear Zeus, down on the ploughland of the Athenians and the plains.” Either one should not pray, or one should pray like this: simply and like a free person.
single.label: A practice · how to pray
single.t: If I pray, I pray simply and like a free person, as the Athenians prayed for rain on their land.
single.why: Only this passage speaks of prayer. It says how to pray, not for whom.
single.follows: If one prays at all, one should pray as in this prayer: simply and like a free person.

single.quote: It should not lean on the obstacles it meets with force or like a torrent, nor fall down, but stand and light up whatever receives it. For whatever does not give the beam passage will deprive itself of the beam.
single.label: Meeting an obstacle
single.t: When something stands in my way, I do not force my way and I do not fall. I stand and give light to whatever receives it; what gives the light no passage deprives itself of it.
single.why: Only this passage says how to meet what resists me. It shows what failing looks like, forcing or falling, and the way back.
single.follows: Meeting an obstacle, thought should neither force its way nor fall, but stand and light up what receives it.

members.text:
The earth, saith the poet, doth often long after the rain. So is
the glorious sky often as desirous to fall upon the earth, which argues
a mutual kind of love between them. And so (say I) doth the world bear
a certain affection of love to whatsoever shall come to pass With thine
affections shall mine concur, O world. The same (and no other) shall the
object of my longing be which is of thine. Now that the world doth love
it is true indeed so is it as commonly said, and acknowledged ledged,
when, according to the Greek phrase, imitated by the Latins, of things
that used to be, we say commonly, that they love to be.
members.english: “The earth loves the rain, and the holy sky loves,” and the universe loves to bring about whatever is to come. So I say to the universe: “I love along with you.” And is that, too, perhaps said in this sense: “this loves to happen”?

Whatsoever is expedient unto thee, O World, is expedient unto me;
nothing can either be 'unseasonable unto me, or out of date, which unto
thee is seasonable. Whatsoever thy seasons bear, shall ever by me be
esteemed as happy fruit, and increase. O Nature! from thee are all
things, in thee all things subsist, and to thee all tend. Could he say
of Athens, Thou lovely city of Cecrops; and shalt not thou say of the
world, Thou lovely city of God?
members.english: Universe, everything that fits well with you fits well with me. Nothing that is timely for you is too early or too late for me. Nature, everything your seasons bear is fruit to me. upon him to do that which belongs to the rain? or his son Aesculapius

members.text:
The sun seemeth to be shed abroad. And indeed it is diffused but
not effused. For that diffusion of it is a τάσις or an extension. For
therefore are the beams of it called ἀκτῖνες from the word ἐκτείνεσθαι
to be stretched out and extended. Now what a sunbeam is, thou mayest
know if thou observe the light of the sun, when through some narrow
hole it pierceth into some room that is dark. For it is always in a
direct line. And as by any solid body, that it meets with in the way
that is not penetrable by air, it is divided and abrupted, and yet
neither slides off, or falls down, but stayeth there nevertheless: such
must the diffusion in the mind be; not an effusion, but an extension.
What obstacles and impediments soever she meeteth within her way, she
must not violently, and by way of an impetuous onset light upon them;
neither must she fall down; but she must stand, and give light unto
that which doth admit of it. For as for that which doth not, it is its
own fault and loss, if it bereave itself of her light.
members.english: The sun seems to be poured down, and indeed it is poured in every direction, yet it is not poured out. For this pouring is an extension; its beams, at any rate, are called aktines (“rays”) from ekteinesthai (“to be extended”). You could see what a ray is if you watched the sun’s light coming through something narrow into a shaded room. For it extends in a straight line and leans, so to speak, against whatever solid thing it meets that shuts off the air beyond; there it stands, and it does not slip down or fall. So the pouring and spreading of thought should be like that: in no way a pouring out, but an extension. It should not lean on the obstacles it meets with force or like a torrent, nor fall down, but stand and light up whatever receives it. For whatever does not give the beam passage will deprive itself of the beam.
members.greek: Ὁ ἥλιος κατακεχύσθαι δοκεῖ καὶ πάντῃ γε κέχυται, οὐ μὴν ἐκκέχυται. ἡ γὰρ χύσις αὕτη τάσις ἐστίν· ἀκτῖνες γοῦν αἱ αὐγαὶ αὐτοῦ ἀπὸ τοῦ ἐκτείνεσθαι λέγονται. ὁποῖον δέ τι ἐστὶν ἀκτίς, ἴδοις ἄν, εἰ διά τινος στενοῦ εἰς ἐσκιασμένον οἶκον τὸ ἀφ’ ἡλίου φῶς εἰσδυόμενον θεάσαιο· τείνεται γὰρ κατ’ εὐθὺ καὶ ὥσπερ διερείδεται πρὸς τὸ στερέμνιον ὅ τι ἂν ἀπαντήσῃ διεῖργον τὸν ἐπέκεινα ἀέρα, ἐνταῦθα δὲ ἔστη καὶ οὐ κατώλισθεν οὐδὲ ἔπεσε. τοιαύτην οὖν τὴν χύσιν καὶ διάχυσιν τῆς διανοίας εἶναι χρή, μηδαμῶς ἔκχυσιν, ἀλλὰ τάσιν, καὶ πρὸς τὰ ἀπαντῶντα κωλύματα μὴ βίαιον μηδὲ ῥαγδαίαν τὴν ἐπέρεισιν ποιεῖσθαι μηδὲ μὴν καταπίπτειν, ἀλλὰ ἵστασθαι καὶ ἐπιλάμπειν τὸ δεχόμενον· αὐτὸ γὰρ ἑαυτὸ στερήσει τῆς αὐγῆς τὸ μὴ παραπέμπον αὐτήν.

members.text:
The form of the Athenians' prayer did run thus: 'O rain, rain, good
Jupiter, upon all the grounds and fields that belong to the Athenians.'
Either we should not pray at all, or thus absolutely and freely; and not
every one for himself in particular alone.
members.english: A prayer of the Athenians: “Rain, rain, dear Zeus, down on the ploughland of the Athenians and the plains.” Either one should not pray, or one should pray like this: simply and like a free person.

decisions: Quotes the project’s own translation from the Greek instead of Casaubon. Passage numbers stay Casaubon’s. In modern editions 10.21 is 10.20, 10.22 is 10.21, 4.19 is 4.23, 6.38 is 6.43 and 8.54 is 8.57; 5.7 is the same.
Reads “the nature of the whole” (10.21), the universe and nature addressed in 4.19, and the universe of 10.22 as one whole.

Keeps only two fused claims. In claim 1 both passages say that what nature brings is good for the one it is brought to, and both speak of its time. In claim 2 the words the two share, “I take the universe’s side”, are the editor’s summary of two sentences spoken to the universe. The parts of the world working together (6.38) and all things from, in and into nature (4.19) are each said by one passage and stand alone.
Withdraws the earlier claim that I pray “for everyone, not for myself alone”. It rested on a clause Casaubon added to 5.7; the Greek ends at “simply and like a free person”.
Reads “Dear city of Zeus” (4.19) as said of the world. The Greek does not say what the city of Zeus is.
Leaves out the poet’s line and the last sentence of 10.22, a remark on a Greek turn of phrase.
articles.limit: Article 3 already says that I accept whatever happens. What this article adds is the time: what comes is good when it comes, never too early or too late. It adds little else. Six passages give two fused claims, and 4.19 feeds both, so the article leans on one passage. It states a trust and does not argue for it.
